utterances.speaker: JUDGE POCAR
utterances.text: Good morning, everybody. Madam Registrar, may I ask you to call the case.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honours. Good morning everyone in and around the courtroom. This is case number IT-00-39-A, the Prosecutor versus Momcilo Krajisnik.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE POCAR
utterances.text: I thank you. May I ask Mr. Krajisnik if he can hear me and follow the proceedings through the translation. THE APPELLANT: [Interpretation] Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE POCAR
utterances.text: Thank you. Now let me call for appearances. For Mr. Krajisnik's counsel on the matter of JCE, please. MR. N. DERSHOWITZ: Nathan Dershowitz --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, please. MR. N. DERSHOWITZ: Nathan Dershowitz.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE POCAR
utterances.text: I thank you. And for the Prosecution, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. KREMER
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. President. Peter Kremer appearing with Julian Nicholls, Mr. Alan Tieger, and our case manager this morning is Mr. Iain Reid.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE POCAR
utterances.text: Thank you. For the amicus curiae. MR. C. NICHOLLS: Colin Nicholls appearing with Michelle Butler.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE POCAR
utterances.text: Today we resume the evidentiary hearing on appeal in the case of the Prosecutor against Momcilo Krajisnik. At the outset, you recall that Monday the Prosecutor inquired about a word limit for the supplemental briefs. The parties and the amicus curiae are allowed to file on any impact of exhibits AD1 and AD2, the rebuttal evidence and the viva voce evidence of Mr. Mano and Mr. Karganovic, and on any impact on Mr. Karadzic's testimony during today's hearing. As both supplemental briefs are due on 14 November 2008, the Appeals Chamber had decided that they be filed in a consolidated filing, which shall not exceed 7.500 words. Now, the purpose of today's hearing is to hear the testimony of Radovan Karadzic, who has been admitted as a witness under Rule 115 of the Rules in the Appeals Chamber's decision of 16 October 2008. On 31st October 2008, Mr. Krajisnik filed a summary of facts on which Mr. Karadzic will testify during today's hearing. On 3 November 2008, Mr. Krajisnik requested the Appeals Chamber to admit into evidence, pursuant to Rule 92 ter of the Rules, a written statement of Mr. Karadzic, which is identical to the summary of facts filed on 31st October 2008 except for one deletion. On the same day, the Appeals Chamber decided that this written statement should be admitted under Rule 92 ter of the Rules at today's hearing provided that the requirements set forth in Rule 92 ter are met, that is, that Mr. Karadzic is present and is available for cross-examination and other questioning by the Judges, and will attest that the written judgement -- the written statement accurately reflects his declaration and what he would say if examined. We will proceed in the following order this morning: First, Mr. Karadzic will be asked by the appellant whether he attests that the written statement accurately reflects his declaration and what he would say if examined. Subsequently, the Prosecution may cross-examine Mr. Karadzic for one and a half hours, and the Defence may re-examine the witness for 45 minutes. Should the appellant wish counsel on the matter of JCE to re-examine Karadzic on his behalf with regard to the issue of joint criminal enterprise, this examination has to be made within the time allotted for the appellant. We will rise for the usual breaks. The time allotted to the parties are approximate, as usual, and may with leave of the Chamber be extended if necessary. That said, I wish to remind the parties they are not obliged to use all the time allotted. As always, the Judges may interrupt at any time to ask questions to the witness. After the questioning by the Judges, the written statement will be admitted into evidence pursuant to Rule 92 ter of the Rules. Now I would like to call witness Radovan Karadzic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE POCAR
utterances.text: Good morning, Mr. Karadzic. Can you hear me in a language you understand?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE POCAR
utterances.text: Thank you. Could you now please read the solemn declaration given to you by the usher.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE POCAR
utterances.text: Thank you. You may now be seated. Could you please tell the Court your full name and date of birth.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Radovan Karadzic, the 19th of June, 1945.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE POCAR
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Karadzic. Before we begin, I noted on 23rd October 2008 the registrar assigned Mr. Peter Robinson as your counsel for the purposes of this evidentiary hearing. May I please ask counsel for Mr. Karadzic for his appearance.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes, thank you, Mr. President. Good morning and good morning to members of the Appeals Chamber. I'm Peter Robinson, counsel for President Karadzic. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE POCAR
utterances.text: Thank you. I would like to inform you, Mr. Robinson, that, as is usual practice, you may make interventions concerning your client's rights but not in relation to the factual basis on his testimony. Now, Mr. Karadzic, you have been summoned to testify in the appeal proceedings in the case of the Prosecutor against Momcilo Krajisnik. You have prepared a written statement, and the appellant will ask you in a moment whether this accurately reflects what you said and what you would say if examined. Afterwards, the Prosecution will pose its questions to you, and then you will be re-examined by Mr. Krajisnik or his counsel on the matter of JCE. Please also note that the Judges may ask you questions at any point of this hearing. Now I want to add this: Given that you are an accused person before this Tribunal, I have to alert you that you have the right to remain silent if you feel at any time that the questions asked of you may require you to give information that may incriminate you. In such instances, irrespective of who is asking you the question, you have a right to ask the Appeals Chamber to exempt you from answering such questions. Do you understand this advice that I have just explained?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, and I would rely on my counsel for that and his advice.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE POCAR
utterances.text: Thank you. There is one more thing I need to mention. You are currently detained in the UN Detention Unit together with the appellant, Mr. Momcilo Krajisnik. Therefore, the Registrar was directed to order your segregation from Mr. Krajisnik for the duration of your testimony here, after which the segregation will stop. The Chamber has been informed by the Registry that this segregation is being carried out today. Are you aware of this segregation, and if so, do you understand the meaning of this segregation?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, fully.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE POCAR
utterances.text: Thank you. Well, I now will give the floor to the Defence for Mr. Momcilo Krajisnik.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRAJISNIK
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning, Mr. Karadzic. My first question has to do with procedure. You have before you the statement signed, so my first question is: Is that indeed your statement?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN KARADZIC
utterances.text: May I just receive that statement, please. Yes, that is my statement.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRAJISNIK
utterances.text: Can you attest to the Trial Chamber that that statement is accurate and that it accurately reflects what you would say here in court were you to testify?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN KARADZIC
utterances.text: Yes, fully.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRAJISNIK
utterances.text: My third question is this: Do you agree to place yourself at the disposal of the Prosecution today for a cross-examination, and would you allow the Trial Chamber to ask you additional questions and indeed anybody else who has the right by procedure to ask you questions?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN KARADZIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRAJISNIK
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, I hope I have fulfilled my procedural obligation and that the proceedings can continue. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE POCAR
utterances.text: I thank you, Mr. Krajisnik. I believe now we can ask the Prosecutor to start the cross-examination.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President, Your Honours. Good morning.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Good morning, Mr. Karadzic.

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN KARADZIC
utterances.text: Good morning.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Mr. Karadzic, your statement at page 12 asserts that the Bosnian Serb leadership had no policy of ethnic separation. During the course of the trial, over 31 months, there was a great deal of evidence adduced that in many, many municipalities within Republika Srpska or the areas claimed by Republika Srpska in 1992 that the forces of the army of Republika Srpska, the VRS, and the Ministry of the Interior, the MUP, forcibly transferred, detained on a massive scale under inhumane conditions, murdered, exterminated Bosnian Muslims and Croats. My question is: Do you deny that those crimes took place, acknowledge that those crimes took place, or assert that you do not know?

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBINSON
utterances.text: Excuse me, Mr. President. I would like to make an intervention at this time and ask you to exempt Mr. Karadzic from answering that question, and if I may make a brief submission on that point. Mr. Karadzic is here to testify to the involvement of Mr. Krajisnik in the various organs as set forth in his statement, and as you know, he has his own trial yet to face at which the issues encompassed by Mr. Tieger's question will be fully explored, but this is not the time and place for that. Under Rule 90(H), you have the discretion to control the proceedings by requiring only questions to be answered relevant to the case being heard before the Appeals Chamber, and initially, I simply ask you to exercise your discretion under Rule 90(H) and exempt Mr. Karadzic from answering that question. In the event that the Chamber is not willing to do that, then we will invoke another provision of Rule 90. Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE POCAR
utterances.text: I consulted my colleagues. You're exempt from answering this question.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Mr. Karadzic, your statement asserts that the A and B variants document, as you called it, which is P64A, tab 390, in evidence, was an ordinary pamphlet drafted by mostly elderly men, had essentially nothing to do with the SDS and that the SDS never attempted to implement it. Now, first of all, P64A, tab 390, the A and B document, is formally entitled, "The instructions for the organisation and operation of organs of the Serbian people in Bosnia and Herzegovina in emergency conditions." It's dated 19 December 1991 and is headed "Serbian Democratic Party, SDS, of Bosnia and Herzegovina, Main Board." And as I think you alluded to in your statement, at least by the description, it's a document that contains two variants, A and B, representing municipalities in which Serbs were a majority and municipalities in which Serbs were a minority, and two levels or stages of activation. Now, with respect to your assertion that this was a pamphlet prepared by elderly men with nothing to do with the SDS, let me direct your attention to some of the evidence in this case and ask if you acknowledge that or deny that or are unaware of it. P529, tab 49, was a statement at the 50th session of the Bosnian Serb Assembly in April 1995, made by you, Dr. Karadzic, as follows: "At the moment the war began in the municipalities where we were in the majority, we had municipal power, held it firmly, controlled everything. In the municipalities where we were in the minority, we set up secret government, Municipal Boards, Municipal Assemblies, presidents of executive boards. You will remember the A and B variants. In the B variant where we were in the minority, 20 per cent, 15 per cent, we set up a government and a brigade, a unit, no matter what size, but there was a detachment with a commander. Distribution of weapons was carried out thanks to the JNA," and so on. Mr. Karadzic, do you acknowledge that you said that? Do you deny that you said that, or do you not recall?

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBINSON
utterances.text: Excuse me, Mr. President. Again I'm going to ask you under Rule 90(H) to except Mr. Karadzic from answering that question because, again, he's here to help the Appeals Chamber clarify the role of Mr. Krajisnik, and bearing in mind that he has his own case in which these statements and issues will be aired, we would ask you that you exercise your discretion and exempt him from answering the question. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE POCAR
utterances.text: Again, Mr. Tieger, I consulted my colleagues, and we are of the view that Mr. Karadzic should be exempted from the question.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Your Honour --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE POCAR
utterances.text: You should explain which these questions relate to the position of Mr. Krajisnik.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Your Honours, this goes to --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE POCAR
utterances.text: And not of the accused himself -- the witness himself as an accused.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Your Honour, as it was made clear during the course of the trial, the accused and Mr. Krajisnik walked hand-in-hand through the process of the establishment of the structures, the implementation of the policies, and the pursuit of the objectives. Every question related to this witness's credibility will necessarily touch upon the issues in his statement. It's Mr. Karadzic in his statement who raised the question of Variant A and B, not the Prosecution, who asserted a position with respect to that document. Surely the Prosecution is entitled to confront him with evidence in the case that it asserts is incompatible, inconsistent, and belies the statement -- or the assertions made in his statement. It's a classic confrontation on a credibility issue, and the -- I don't believe that the witness should be entitled to proffer a statement to the Court to tell the Court, "This is what I say happened," and then turn around and hide behind an assertion of self-incrimination after he's just fundamentally waived that by making the very assertion in his statement. He's the one who said, "This is the nature of this document." Surely the Prosecution is entitled to confront him with evidence to the contrary.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE POCAR
utterances.text: Can you give us the exact reference in the statement?

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: It's on page 13, Your Honour. And it would begin with the third paragraph under the heading on that page.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE POCAR
utterances.text: Mr. Tieger, we considered your submission, but the question, the way you put it may be taken as extracting information that may be self-incriminating. So if the -- if the witness invokes that point, that reason I think he should be exempted.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: First of all, Your Honour, I believe the invocation was to 90(H) on relevance. I think it's clear that this question is relevant. So if that is the basis for the invocation, I would ask the Court to overrule it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE POCAR
utterances.text: Mr. Robinson. I heard Mr. Robinson invoking the two reasons, although one as the second one.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes, I was invoking first your discretion under Rule 90(H). In the event that you feel this is something you would like to hear, then we would be invoking Mr. Karadzic's rights under Article 21(4)(g), that evidence not be used against him, and under Rule 90(E). And when you're confronting him with a prior statement, just acknowledging the prior statement itself can be used against him in his trial and relieve the Prosecution of the burden of establishing that, and therefore, we ask that he be exempted if not under 90(H), then these other Rules and Articles. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE POCAR
utterances.text: So I correctly interpreted your submission. Thank you. Please continue, Mr. Tieger.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Mr. Karadzic, please tell the Trial Chamber whether you are aware if anyone in the Bosnian Serb leadership or during the course of Assembly sessions, municipal and Executive Board sessions, deputies club sessions which you attended invoked Variant A -- the Variant A and B document and mentioned the Variant A and B document. MR. N. DERSHOWITZ: Your Honour, if I -- if I may. Solely in terms of JCE and the thrust of the assertion, I would object to questions unless there's some indication that Mr. Krajisnik was present or had any knowledge or involvement or anything else, but to the extent that it deals solely with events that have no connection to this defendant and the charges against him and the JCE elements, I would object to them. And then I have an inquiry, and my only inquiry is I will try to object solely in terms of JCE. I just wanted to confirm that that's my role not to object any broader than that.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Your Honour, if I may --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE POCAR
utterances.text: Mr. Dershowitz, I believe the question as it has been put can be put, actually, and we can't -- depends on the line of questioning that the Prosecutor's intending follow. I mean, this maybe relevant for -- in light of the line of questioning the Prosecution is taking. So I believe the question should be admitted. Please, Mr. Karadzic, you can -- if you can answer the question.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] In order for the full truth to come out, I have to expand my answer a little bit. Although my Defence counsel has advised me not to answer that question, it is true that this is not a document originating from the Serbian Democratic Party. It is true that the officers, when they -- when their apartments were being put on the list and they -- their lives came into danger, they came closer to the positions of the SDS and --

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Your Honour, may I object. May I object, please. Excuse me, Mr. Karadzic. I'm sorry to interrupt but I'm trying to ... It's clearly not a platform for the witness to provide information that he may, at the moment, deem of interest. Questions are being put to the witness. I would ask that he answer it.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBINSON
utterances.text: Excuse me, Mr. President. I believe that the witness ought to be able to make a complete answer to the questions that are being put to him. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Your Honour, that's not an answer, it's a filibuster and there is no answer to the question. The Prosecution has 90 minutes to pursue its examination. I'm trying to present the Court with as much relevant evidence as possible, and I would ask that the witness simply answer the question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE POCAR
utterances.text: Yes. Please, Mr. Karadzic, just answer the questions that are put to you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could you please repeat your question.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Mr. Karadzic, the question was: At any of the deputies club sessions, Assembly sessions, meetings of the Municipal and Executive Board members, party gatherings, did you hear members of the Bosnian Serb leadership or members of those gatherings refer to or invoke the A and B document?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN KARADZIC
utterances.text: Yes. It's possible that that was the case, but that was not a party document. That was a document that we did not have any right to keep confidential, so we circulated it.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: And when you say, "We circulated it," who circulated it and when was it circulated?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN KARADZIC
utterances.text: It was passed -- it was actually brought to a meeting of the Serbian Democratic Party and I asked someone to provide explanations. They did not want to provide a statement of reasons. We did not have time to discuss it and to adopt it. We simply circulated it because we did not have the right to conceal from the people something that might have a bearing on the defence of the people.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: And did any Bosnian Serb leader advise members of the party at any gathering to implement the document, either stage 1 or stage 2?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN KARADZIC
utterances.text: Well, I don't have the document here before me, so I don't know what stages 1 or 2 would entail, but it is quite possible that at the time when war was looming, it is possible that a recommendation was made for the material that had been studied by the military circles, by the -- all the officers to be taken into account. Naturally had the war not occurred, it would make no sense had the conference on the reorganisation of Bosnia succeeded, had everyone accepted the Lisbon Agreement as we had, then it would all have been moot.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: That wasn't my question, Mr. Karadzic, and I believe you know it. The question is whether any member of the Bosnian Serb leadership told the party members to implement stage 1 or stage 2.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBINSON
utterances.text: Excuse me, Mr. President. If I could just make a small intervention at this point. I don't believe that it's appropriate when Mr. Tieger comments that he believes that Mr. Karadzic knows the answer or to suggest that he's evading an answer. I don't think that's a professional conduct that we should have in the Appeals Chamber. So I would ask that he direct him when he makes a question not to give his own opinion or comment on the -- his view of the way the evidence is going. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: The evidence is not going, Your Honour, because I'm not getting answers to the question.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: And the question was: Did any of the party members tell members of the party to, for example, activate level 2 or stage 2 of the A and B document?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN KARADZIC
utterances.text: It is quite possible, but now whether this was this document or something else, I cannot tell you because I did not attend all the meetings. If we're talking about the A and B variant document and it was presented, then it's possible, but I can't really tell you. I don't know that. So I have to be clear about what stage was recommended, what measures, what document, and in what circumstances and in what context.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Members of the party received the A and B document from the Main Board of which Mr. Krajisnik and you were members, in fact of which you were the president, and implemented it. Isn't that correct?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN KARADZIC
utterances.text: Well, in most municipalities it was not implemented, in fact.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: In how many municipalities was it implemented, Mr. Karadzic?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN KARADZIC
utterances.text: I think it was not fully implemented in any of the municipalities. Perhaps some of the defence measures implemented in some of the municipalities may correspond to the measures proposed in this military document, I don't know that, but I'm sure that the paper was not implemented in full anywhere. In most of the municipalities none of it was implemented and some of it may have been implemented in some municipalities.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: And where it was implemented, to whatever extent, it was implemented because it was distributed by the Main Board and its authority and acted upon for that reason at the party's direction. Isn't that correct?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN KARADZIC
utterances.text: But not in accordance with this document, with this paper. The leadership, the authorities on the ground did not follow the instructions of the party. First of all because the state apparatus was not party based. People who were in key positions in municipalities such as the police, the judiciary and so on were not party members. And the municipalities as units had their powers in the sphere of defence, Territorial Defence, as part of the All Peoples Defence and social self-protection which was the defence doctrine during Tito's Yugoslavia. So they had full autonomy in this respect.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: The Variant A and B document was distributed by the Main Board at a meeting on or about December 20th. Isn't that right?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN KARADZIC
utterances.text: No. This document arrived there at that time, and we allowed it to circulate, but this was not our document. It was not looked at by the organs. It was not discussed. It was not adopted. It was simply an expert opinion proffered by frightened officers who had witnessed the genocide in 1941 and who considered that the people should not be left without any precautionary measures. So it was of a defensive character, and we allowed it to be circulated. But this was not our document. We did not circulate it. We did not send it. And you can see that the signatory is not the Main Board. You can see the heading "The Main Board," but down there it says "The Crisis Staff." That's the signatory, and we didn't know who was supposed to circulate it. We did not even retype it. It was circulated in the same form that it was received by us.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Let me draw your attention to a few documents in evidence, Mr. Karadzic. P529, tab 41, minutes of the 6th meeting of the Executive Committee of the SDS Municipal Board in Kljuic. Item 1, and this is from December 23rd, 1991, very shortly after the Variant A and B document was distributed. "Veljko Kondic informed the meeting of the instructions for the organisation and activities of the Serbian people in Bosnia and Herzegovina. All organs will be required to act in accordance with the instructions. Whoever is not ready to fulfil his duties should say so immediately and it will not be held against him." P529, tab 378, December 23rd. "The meeting held in the premises of the Novo Sarajevo Serbian Democratic Party heard and discussed the materials, received the materials discussed by the SDS Bosnia-Herzegovina Main Board. First degree and assignments were distributed accordingly." P529, tab 42, December 27th. Minutes of the 3rd session of the Executive Committee of Bosanska Krupa, agenda item 3. "The chairman briefed those present on the instruction on establishing SDS Crisis Staffs in Bosnia-Herzegovina and in accordance with the set instruction proposed the establishment of a Crisis Staff. This was followed by establishment of the Crisis Staff of the following make-up." P529, tab 43. SDS Crisis Staff for the city of Sarajevo. "The individual duties according to the instructions on the organisation and activities of the Serb people of Bosnia and Herzegovina in a state of emergency based on version B, first level are as follows," and then there are -- there's a list. Dr. Karadzic, do you deny that those SDS members received the SDS -- received the Variant A and B document from the Main Board at a meeting attended by the Bosnian Serb leadership, in fact presided over by the Bosnian Serb leadership, and then acted in accordance with those instructions as they were told?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN KARADZIC
utterances.text: This document was circulated at the time when a big session was held, attended by about 200 to 300 people. It was a Plenary Session. And the fact that some of the Municipal Boards, two or three of them, found this paper useful, the paper that originated from military expert, does not tell us that this was an instruction or an order from the Main Board of the Serbian Democratic Party. They simply found it expedient to look at this document and to see whether they might find it useful in terms of the security of the people in the -- the citizens in their municipality. It was not a secret paper, secret document. We simply let anyone who wished read this paper, and look at it the way they saw fit.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Mr. Krajisnik was at that meeting, sitting next to you; correct?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN KARADZIC
utterances.text: I don't know that, but this meeting has nothing to do with the paper. The paper was distributed. It was circulated like any other document or paper. It was not a legal instrument. It was not a document originating from the Main Board. It was not distributed on behalf and in the name of the Main Board. And I don't recall who sat on the Presidency at that time. I really don't recall. There were about 300 people at that meeting.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: P529, 385 is another document received in evidence, Mr. Karadzic. That's an intercepted phone call between you and Mr. Cizmovic on 16 January 1992 in which you discuss the state of preparation and the level of cooperation of various municipalities. Mr. Cizmovic says they are prepared for full cooperation. "It's the same with Northern Bosnia. I've prepared a small sort of questionnaire for all of them." And then he says: "What have they managed to do? How far have they come? To what extent are they prepared to implement the first level of the instructions?" That was Mr. Cizmovic talking about the Variant A and B document, wasn't it, Mr. Karadzic?

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBINSON
utterances.text: Excuse me, Mr. President. I'm going to interpose an objection to any question that asks Mr. Karadzic to, in a sense, authenticate an intercepted conversation or a document because that could be used against him and relieve the Prosecution of the burden of establishing that at his trial. So pursuant to Article 21(g) and Rule 95(E), I ask that you exempt him from answering that question. Also pursuant to Rule 90(H), on the issue of relevance. I noticed we've spent 30 minutes now and barely mentioned Mr. Krajisnik, which is the purpose for Mr. Karadzic has come here, and so I also ask you to consider exercising your discretion to ask Mr. Tieger to move on to a more relevant line of questioning. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE POCAR
utterances.text: Well, if you invoke the reason that this may incriminate your client, I think we -- Mr. Karadzic has to be exempted from answering.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBINSON
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. And if I can just mention one other thing at this point and that is the other part of Rule 90(E) which allows you to direct the witness to answer and the -- after you making such direction the result is his answers could not be used against him in his own case, and I invite the Prosecutor, if it's truly interested in having these answers, to make an application for you to invoke that Rule. And if they do that, then Mr. Karadzic is prepared to answer all of their questions, but they should not be allowed under the guise of this hearing for Mr. Krajisnik to be trying to enhance their position in his case, which seems to me to have been the entire gist of all these questions you've heard so far. So I invite the Prosecution to make an application under Rule 90(E). If you grant it, you can have the answers to all of these questions. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: One quick response, Your Honour. First of all, I'm not going to comment on the procedure, but the questions I've asked, number one, were raised by the witness's statement. They're matters that go to credibility. And number two, they're matters that go to the activities of the Bosnian Serb leadership, their efforts to implement policy, their -- and objectives, their control over the party. It's of course highly relevant. I will be moving on because I have limited time. However, it's absolutely false to suggest that any questions that go to matters raised by this witness in his statement that touch upon the activities of the Bosnian Serb leadership of which Mr. Krajisnik was a member, which is the heart of the case, is not relevant. This matter was -- was relevant both in terms of creditability and in terms of the activities and efforts of the Bosnian Serb leadership. Let me move on to the War Presidency, however, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Mr. Karadzic, your statement asserts that the June 2nd document providing for the possibility of expanding the Presidency in a time of war, that is a wartime or expanded Presidency was never put into effect and that Mr. Krajisnik simply attended Presidency meetings like any other invitee, and he was not a member. Now, it's true, however, and it's one thing that's not mentioned in your statement, that Mr. Krajisnik is explicitly identified as a member of the Presidency in the minutes of the sessions and in a number of the minutes of the sessions of the Presidency of Republika Srpska; correct?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN KARADZIC
utterances.text: No, it's not correct. Substantively speaking, the minutes endeavoured -- well, usually after the meetings, after the sessions, the heading was written by the secretary. They weren't sessions of the expanded Presidency but expanded meetings of the Presidency, and this could not be done without the conditions written down in the constitution and the laws. Now, our minutes from the Presidency sessions were compiled in different ways, and usually they were done by secretaries, male and female --

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Mr. Karadzic, excuse me. Excuse me. You've had a chance to put your assertions in your statement, now it's my opportunity to ask you specific questions within a limited time. So my question is, and let me turn your attention to specific minutes, P65, Treanor 13, tab 154. That's the minutes of the 21st Presidency session held on 2 August, and in those minutes reference is made to "Members of the negotiating delegation who are also members of the Presidency (Dr. Karadzic, Dr. Koljevic, and Mr. Krajisnik)." That's an explicit reference to Mr. Krajisnik as a member of the Presidency; correct?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN KARADZIC
utterances.text: That is an imprecision of the person who kept the minutes. It is of no importance. The members of the Presidency were Mr. Koljevic and I.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: And, Dr. Karadzic, you signed those minutes; correct?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN KARADZIC
utterances.text: The minutes weren't acts and documents of the Presidency. Those were orders, decisions, conclusions. The minutes are something that are quite unimportant. They just represent notes about what was said at the meeting. It's not an official legal document of the Presidency. It's just a set of notes compiled by a person who does not have extensive knowledge about state government and state administration. So I would never rely on minutes. You shouldn't take them as being that important. You should look at the decisions. You should look at the conclusions. The official documents and acts of the Presidency as passed according to its constitutional remit.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: We will look at some statements in a moment, but I take it the answer to that question is yes because that's what the document reveals, and I'll ask you the following questions as well: The minutes of the 23rd Presidency session --

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN KARADZIC
utterances.text: Just a moment. Just a moment. I don't know what yes, what are you saying, because Krajisnik was not a member of the Presidency, and the minutes are not a document on the basis of which you can conclude that. As I say, minutes are an unimportant note on the basis of what was discussed, but decisions, conclusions, orders are official Presidency documents. So the minutes of itself mean nothing, because they are kept by somebody who does not have a lot of knowledge about the constitution and state administration.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Is it correct that the minutes, I just ask you about the 21st session, is it correct that the minutes of the 23rd Presidency session, P64, P65, Treanor 13, tab 186, list Mr. Krajisnik explicitly as a member of the Presidency or don't you know?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN KARADZIC
utterances.text: Well, I'd like see the document. And let me state again, why at the 26th session would somebody write "member" by his name and not having -- not written that in the first session or the first 25 sessions? So it's just lack of skill on the part -- or lack of knowledge on the part of the person keeping the minutes. And as I say once again, the minutes are not a document. It's just an aide-memoire about what happened, and on the basis of the minutes the secretary writes the orders or I do and I sign it but as I say, minutes are unimportant. They're not vital for you to be able to draw conclusions on the basis of minutes. It is just an unimportant aide-memoire of what happened at any particular meeting.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: In fact, Mr. Karadzic, it's true, isn't it, that Mr. Krajisnik is indicated as a member of the Presidency on seven of the sessions -- of minutes of the sessions of the Presidency which were held, all of which you signed except for one which was signed by Mr. Krajisnik as presiding. Isn't that right?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN KARADZIC
utterances.text: No, it's not right. The minutes that you're referring to, I saw them during the proofing session, and it wasn't a Presidency session. Two members were not there. There was one Presidency member, and while they were waiting for us they held an unofficial discussion which they recorded, but you'll see that in those minutes there's not a single decision, conclusion, order, or official document from the Presidency's domain, which is passed by the Presidency. So it wasn't a Presidency session at all, and it was signed there that such-and-such a discussion had taken place but nothing was passed, no decisions made. And they couldn't have been because the two of us did not manage to arrive at the meeting. So I'm afraid you're attaching too much importance to minutes which mean nothing. They're just the notes written down by a secretary, nothing more than that.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Mr. Karadzic, the Trial Chamber had an opportunity to review those minutes in detail, as has the Appellate Chamber. You were referring to the October 9th session on which you were not present -- at which you were not present, and in fact the only persons present were Mr. Karadzic -- excuse me, Mr. Krajisnik, Mr. Djeric, and Ms. Plavsic; is that right? And the October 9th session is listed as a Presidency session, Mr. Krajisnik is explicitly indicated as a member, and Mr. Krajisnik signed that document as presiding. That's correct, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN KARADZIC
utterances.text: No, it's not correct that it was a Presidency session, because the two of us did not manage to arrive at the session. They were expecting us, and while they were expecting us they had a discussion and looked into various matters, made recommendations, but they could not pass any decisions. They couldn't because the Presidency was not sitting in a quorum. There was no quorum. So that's the essence of the matter. Had we arrived at the Presidency session, it would have been a Presidency session. Like this it wasn't, and those were notes about consultations held compiled by one Presidency member with the invitees at the meeting, at the session.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Mr. Karadzic, your statement says that the --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE POCAR
utterances.text: [Microphone not activated]

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MERON
utterances.text: Mr. Karadzic, the Trial Chamber found that Mr. Krajisnik was an active member of a five-member Presidency or a de facto member of the expanded Presidency, a finding which you dispute in your statement on page 6. You state that Mr. Krajisnik, and I quote you, "never took part in the 'decision-making process' of the Presidency." Once the decisions of the Presidency were typed up, they were signed by you. That you say on page 4 of your statement. However, the Trial Chamber supported its findings with evidence that on three occasions Mr. Krajisnik himself signed Presidency documents over your printed name. This is stated in paragraph 177 of the trial judgement. How do you account for that, Mr. Karadzic?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The documents that are referred to in that paragraph are not documents appointing someone, nominating someone. They're just confirmation that such-and-such has that capacity, that status. My secretary could have signed it over my name. It's just confirmation that the person appointed to a particular post has that status, and when he received that status, that is a Presidency decision that I -- was signed by me. It wasn't signed by Mr. Koljevic or Mr. -- or Mrs. Plavsic, it was I who signed it and sometimes Mr. Koljevic. So what Mr. Krajisnik signed is not a decision and act of appointment but just in my absence somebody signed and then that person can show it to the municipality and show that he was an official person.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MERON
utterances.text: But what does it suggest about his position as a member of the Presidency, Mr. Karadzic?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] He wasn't a member of the Presidency. My secretary could have signed over my name. Quite simply it is confirmation that the person in question was nominated at some previous point in time, that he was nominated or appointed to a post or function, and it could have been signed by anybody whom people trusted and was well known. Whether it was my secretary or anybody else, it's just confirmation, a certificate, confirmation stating that that person is an official person, has an official capacity.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MERON
utterances.text: That's all.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE POCAR
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Tieger, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Mr. Karadzic, your statement says that the Presidency contemplated on November 30th, 1992, the introduction of an expanded or wartime Presidency but rejected that because the constitutional prerequisites had not been fulfilled, that is, a state of war had not been declared. In fact, Mr. Karadzic, there was the -- the document -- the Presidency session of November 30th makes reference to a parliamentary inquiry, and that's a reference to the session of the 22nd session of the Bosnian Serb Assembly held in Zvornik in late November 1992; correct?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN KARADZIC
utterances.text: The fact is that the deputies asked us for the Presidency to exist, an expanded Presidency, that is, and the need for an expanded Presidency appeared only when the Assembly cannot meet because of a state of war. And so it wasn't an inquiry, it wasn't a parliamentary inquiry, it was a question from the deputies, and we received this deputy question at the Presidency and we had to answer what the substance of it was. And we concluded at that meeting that there were no conditions and no need for an expanded Presidency to be set up because there were no conditions according to the law and under the constitution, so that was about 17 days before we abolished the Presidency and elected a president and two vice-presidents. So that is foolproof that the Presidency did not exist. It's at the end of the '92 mandate and it is proof and evidence, in fact, that the Presidency did not exist whereas the Assembly could meet, and that's why it doesn't exist, and the Presidency could meet because there was no state of war. The Presidency should have had the function of integration and executive power in the absence of the meeting of an Assembly; whereas when the Assembly met, and as it met, there was no need for a Presidency.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Perhaps it will be of assistance to the Chamber to actually look at the session that was held, the 22nd session and what was said there, and that is P65, Treanor 14, tab 213, Your Honour, or P583, Trbojevic tab 106. At that meeting Milan Trbojevic, the deputy Prime Minister, began the discussion on the War Presidency by saying: "The third aspect I would like to mention is the respect for the constitution and the law, the value of law in our state. I find the situation truly tragic. First of all, we have a parallel system of authority, the public and 'legal' wartime Presidency is an organ of authority that isn't mentioned in the constitution. Wartime commissioners working in the field are neither recognised by the constitution nor the law. What this means is that from the top of the state down to the level of the municipality, there is a parallel system of authority." That's what Mr. Trbojevic said, correct, because I want to move on to some other excerpts from that, or don't you know?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN KARADZIC
utterances.text: I don't have the minutes before me, but I do know that that was the culmination of a misunderstanding and conflict between Mr. Trbojevic and Mr. Djeric and some other ministers, but the fact remains that the government asked for commissioners, the commissioners did not have powers and authorities. They had duties to give advice to bodies in the field. We had no telephone connections, that was the reason, and because the people in power and authority along the periphery were not people who used --

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: We'll be speaking about the commissioners in just a moment. Now, after Mr. Trbojevic's intervention you responded, and you said at page 60 of that document: "I was always on the side of the Presidency, not the president. There are only a few of us as it is. If Koljevic and I go somewhere, Biljana remains. At least there's one of the three of us. But if Biljana leaves, then Mr. Krajisnik." And then in response to Mr. Trbojevic's intervention, Mr. Krajisnik said the following at page 100, and remember Mr. Trbojevic had said, "We have a parallel system of authority, the public and legal wartime Presidency." And Mr. Krajisnik said at page 100: "Gentlemen, we received a response to the deputy question on wartime Presidency and commissioners. The question was raised by Mr. Trbojevic and it has been clearly stated that this isn't compliant with the constitution. Wartime Presidency," he went on to say, "consists of three members of the Presidency, the president of the national assembly," that's Mr. Krajisnik, "and the Prime Minister." That's what Mr. Krajisnik said at that 22nd session, isn't it, Mr. Karadzic?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN KARADZIC
utterances.text: But that does not mean that the War Presidency was in force, because there was no state of war, and if -- it says that Koljevic and I were absent, then Mrs. Plavsic is there to inform him or he can be informed by Mr. Krajisnik who knows what went on and what was decided at the meeting. It doesn't mean that he could make decisions. He can just inform him as to what was discussed. So take a look at the minutes of the government and you'll see that the government was completely independent. It had meetings every other day and nobody interfered or meddled. So these talks about parallel power are unfounded.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Let -- why don't we look at what the commissioners said at that session, and those are the commissioners appointed by the Presidency. Now first of all, Mr. Karadzic, let me ask you. The commissioners came into being as a result of the same document that created the Presidency. Isn't that right? The document of -- or excuse me, according to the same law that created the president, based on a decision filed on June 10th, 1992. Or don't you -- don't you remember?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN KARADZIC
utterances.text: No. The need for commissioners arose because the people in the government, in the field, were not skilled in the exercise of power, because during the previous political regime they were dissidents, they were not in power. So this idea to introduce commissioners was brought up by Mr. Djukanovic, a president from another party, the Democratic Party of Federalists, and we took that idea on board. He explained this idea and those people were supposed to be there to support the authorities in the field, in the municipalities and to explain to them what needed to be done. So the government itself saw need for people like that who would explain the documents and the regulations and the laws of the government right there at grassroots level. And those commissioners didn't last long. It was just a very brief period of time.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: But they did exist and on June 10th they existed because you signed a decision, decision on the establishment of War Commissions in municipalities in time of imminent threat of war or during a state of war, and it indicated that War Commissions shall be established. In Article 3: "War Commissions shall maintain the closest possible cooperation with the legal authorities. They shall convey directives issued by the War Presidency of the republic." That's a document you signed, Mr. Karadzic. In Article 4: "State commissioners shall appoint the War Presidencies in consultation with the War Presidency of the republic." Further on in Article 4: "State commissioners shall dissolve the municipal War Presidencies and appoint new members in consultation with the War Presidency of the republic." That's how the commissioners came into being on June 10th, isn't that right, Mr. Karadzic?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN KARADZIC
utterances.text: That was creating conditions for the eventuality of a state of war in which the municipal authorities would not be able to function, the municipal Assemblies would not be able to meet. So we had to create the prerequisites. The legislation had to be in place, decision had been to be in place for the eventuality of the state of war so that the peripheral authorities could function, but this did not eventuate.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: So let me address what these commissioners, apparently fictitious, said at the Zvornik Assembly session in late November 1992. And the first one to speak was Vojo Maksimovic who said at page 103 to 104 of that session: "Sometime at the end of May or beginning of June following a decision issued by our wartime Presidency, wartime commissioners were established for certain regions and deputies were tasked with that duty." Then Mr. Djukanovic spoke at page 105. "I am one of those who participated in the creation of the concept of commissioners and their work and in the establishment of Commissioner's office, and I think I was one of the first commissioners of the wartime Presidency of Republika Srpska." Mr. Karadzic, those commissioners existed notwithstanding the -- the legal technicality to which you continually refer, and they spoke about their existence, their activities and the War Presidency to which they reported on -- at the 22nd session in late November 1992; correct?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN KARADZIC
utterances.text: Mentioning the wartime Presidency is an imprecision on their part, and had the wartime Presidency been established, they would have continued to exist until the end of the state of war. That is a fact. It is also a fact that for a time some of them went to some of the municipalities and established those contacts, but in essence this function was never implemented, and they did not act to any special extent in any of the municipalities because this was just a preparation for the eventuality of a state of war in which the municipal authorities would not be able to function. So this is the substance of it. So if they refer to the wartime Presidency it is an imprecision on their part, but the wartime Presidency was envisaged as were the commissioners in case state of war was declare.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Mr. Krajisnik spoke at some length at that session about the work of the commissioners in a very salutary fashion. He knew they existed. They talked about what they were doing. Isn't that correct?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN KARADZIC
utterances.text: Everybody knew that. Everybody knew that. Why wouldn't they know? The commissioners were not a secret organisation. Commissioners were there as liaison between the Pale government and the periphery, because we did not have telephone communications. And in the municipalities we had people who were not skilled in the exercise of power.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Now, you told the Appellate Chamber that the debate was about whether or not to introduce the War Presidencies, but in fact as we've seen the debate was about whether the existence of the War Presidencies was justified. And if -- it's true, is it not, at P -- well, let me say this, Dr. Karadzic. The Trial Chamber has received evidence, that's P1257, that the minutes of the 22nd session signed by Mr. Krajisnik discussed -- or identified the debate on the question posed at the last session of the Assembly concerning the War Presidency, and those minutes say: "After the discussion it was concluded that the republican Presidency should thoroughly investigate the justification for the existence of the War Presidency." Do you acknowledge that, deny it, or you don't know about those minutes?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN KARADZIC
utterances.text: I think that this was not the case and that there must be a problem with the language, and if I could look at the original document I'll tell you if that is the case.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: We'll find -- we'll get you the document during the break, but this document is in evidence. It's been translated. If there is any problem with the translation, we can -- we can raise that later. Let me -- let me actually mention a --

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN KARADZIC
utterances.text: The interpretation that you've given me, well, that is not correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Well, perhaps we can resolve this by looking at the -- by looking at the session you've referred to in your statement, and that's the 30th November session of the Presidency, P65, Treanor 14, tab 214, you said in your statement that the issue was whether or not to introduce the War Presidency, and in fact the minutes of that session say: "In response to a parliamentary question, the Presidency discussed whether it was justified to introduce a war commission and an extended Presidency under the current circumstances. In both cases," meaning both the war commissioners and the War Presidency, "if these institutions are retained or if we stick with these institutions these regulations must be amended." So -- correct?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN KARADZIC
utterances.text: I would have to look at the original. I'm not sure if this interpretation is correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Well, actually, Mr. Karadzic, Mr. Krajisnik raised that same issue during trial. We -- there was an inquiry made to the interpreters about the word "retained," and the interpretation, and the interpreter staff said the word -- the language in -- in B/C/S meant, "If we stick with," but it definitely did not mean "introduce." Now, if you want to see these documents and do your own review, that's fine, but that's what happened, and that's what the evidence in this case is. It's about sticking with the existing institution, not introducing it for the first time.

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN KARADZIC
utterances.text: Well, I claim here that the War Presidency did not exist because there was not a state of war, and I claim that at that session the debate was about the need to have a wartime Presidency, whether it was necessary or not. If you show me the original document I'll show you where it says so. On the 30th of November, we decided that the conditions were not in place for the wartime Presidency to be introduced. And on the 18th of December, we amended the constitution and elected one president and two vice-presidents. So 17 days before the Presidency ceased to function, we concluded that there was no need, there were no conditions for the wartime Presidency to be established. If I could be given the original minutes I could explain to you the substance, the actual meaning.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Your Honour, I'm looking for the most expeditious way to do this. As I say, this matter was raised during the course of the trial. If the Trial Chamber deems it appropriate, I'm perfectly prepared to do that, but I'm aware of my limited time and I'm about to move on to another subject. I don't want to deprive the Appeals Chamber of a full opportunity that it might wish, but I can direct the Chamber to the portion of the trial transcript at which this same issue was raised.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE POCAR
utterances.text: Well, it's up to you to decide whether you want to go on with this or take up other issues and then direct the Chamber to the transcript.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Mr. Karadzic, I want to move on to some comments you made about the strategic goals which you said in your statement were not military but simply political. First of all, those strategic goals were as published in the Official Gazette on 26 November 1993. That's P29, tab 436. That's decision on strategic objectives for the Serbian people in Bosnia and Herzegovina. The strategic objectives and priorities of the Serbian people in Bosnia and Herzegovina shall be: One, demarcation of the state as separate from the other two national communities. Two, a corridor between Semberija and Krajina. Three, establishment of a corridor in the Drina River valley and the eradication of the Drina River as a border between the Serbian states. Four referred to borders along the rivers Una and Neretva. Five was partition of the city of Sarajevo. And six was access to the sea. And that document is dated 12 May 1992, which is a reference to the 16th Assembly session in Banja Luka on that date. Correct, Mr. Karadzic?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN KARADZIC
utterances.text: The six strategic goals must be looked at within the context of the conference to find a solution for Bosnia and Herzegovina. These objectives were in line with Cutileiro's plan --

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: I'm not asking you yet to expound on your statement, Mr. Karadzic. I want to pose some questions to you in connection with your assertion that the strategic goals were purely political and had no military implications.

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN KARADZIC
utterances.text: First of all, they were not interpreted to me. I wasn't listening to the English but the way they were interpreted back to me does not correspond to the way they were. The first strategic goal was to delineate, demarcate the areas with the other two entities that were envisaged in the Lisbon Agreement. The second strategic goal was to establish a territorial link between the Krajina area and Semberija because the war broke out, although we had tried the units to be compact, the entities to be compact. The third is not the border between the Serb states but the worlds. So we're not talking about the non-existence of the border but the quality of the border. This is what I spoke about on TV in 1993. You have this document where I said this should be a soft border of the kind that we see in Europe. Everything that we presented there was presented during the talks with Ambassador Cutileiro within the talks or, rather, the framework of the Lisbon Agreement. This was not a military document. This was not a secret document. We decided to go public with this document in the media not in the Official Gazette and to send it to the European Community. You have minutes where we -- where we decided that. This was to be our platform in the talks because the conference and the Lisbon Agreement was tabled up until the 26th of August, 1992, although --

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: You are repeating what you've already said in your statement. This is my opportunity to ask you questions relating to that. P529, tab 264, Mr. Karadzic, is a document that details a meeting that was held with presidents of the municipalities in Western Bosnia, and a review of the military and political situation in those municipalities on the 14th of May, 1992, two days after you enunciated the strategic objectives to the Assembly in Banja Luka. There were a number of presidents of the municipal Assemblies and presidents of Serbian municipalities present as well as quite a number of commanders of various brigades and divisions, including Colonel Stanislav Galic, who was then commander of the 30th Partisan Brigade and later became, actually not so long later, became commander of the forces in Sarajevo and ultimately convicted in this institution for his activities there. At that meeting, there was lengthy discussion about activities of the military and what they were doing. Colonel Galic informed those present about the zone of responsibility, the situation and security conditions, and then the president of one of the municipalities presented the conclusions from the meeting held in Banja Luka, listed the strategic objectives, and at the end of the meeting there was a decision among all present that the decisions from the meeting in Banja Luka would be implemented and would be submitted to the commands of the units and to the municipalities. You don't deny that that meeting took place and that discussion took place, do you?

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBINSON
utterances.text: Excuse me, Mr. President. I'm going to at this time invoke first, again, Rule 90(H) because we're once again far afield from Mr. Krajisnik's role, and I think we're essentially in the same position we were with Variant A and B, where the Prosecution is seeking to go into matters that are beyond what is directly relevant to the decision of the Appeals Chamber. So I would ask that you exempt Mr. Karadzic from answering that question and, if not, we would invoke our right under Article 21(4)(g) and Rule 90(E) not to answer that question. And again, I invite the Prosecution if it's important to them and they don't truly intend to use this as an opportunity to build their case against Mr. Karadzic, that they apply to you for an order in which the testimony would not be used against him and then he can answer. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Your Honour, if I could just respond to the relevancy issue and I would simply say this. Thank you for -- no one who participated in this trial could possibly make the assertion that we're far afield from Mr. Krajisnik's role. Number one, there was testimony in the case that Mr. Krajisnik participated in the formulation of the goals; and number two, this is a matter raised by Mr. Karadzic himself and goes directly to his credibility; and number three, it goes to the objectives and the implementation of those objectives by the Bosnian Serb leadership generally. So I think that's far from an accurate assertion.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE POCAR
utterances.text: I accept your point, Mr. Tieger, as far as the relevance is concerned, but as to the point -- the other point made by Mr. Robinson that the answer may incriminate the witness, I have to accept that.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: I believe I can get one more question in before the break, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Same issue, whether the -- the strategic objectives were purely political or military. At P65, tab 182, that's the 17th session of the Bosnian Serb Assembly held in July 1992, that's the first Assembly session after the -- after you enunciated the strategic goals at the 16th session in May, Mr. Kupresanin said this: "This is the Serb Assembly here. It makes decisions. And when I return to Krajina, I want to tell the soldiers, gentlemen, these are our ultimate goals. At the last session in Banja Luka we said that the northern border of the Serb Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina was the right bank of the Sava River. We have come to the realisation that there is a part of Brod left. Bijelo Brdo and Orasje are left. We order the army to realise that goal." You were present at that session. Do you recall that's what Mr. Kupresanin said?

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. President, I'm once again going to ask that we invoke Article 4 -- excuse me, Article 21(4)(g) and Rule 90(E), and again invite the Prosecutor, if he feels this is truly important regarding Mr. Krajisnik, that he ask you to make an order such that it would not be used against Mr. Karadzic at his own trial, and then Mr. Karadzic would be happy to answer that question. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Well, I -- yes, Your Honour. I reject the characterisation of any decision made by the Prosecution to invoke a provision that Defence counsel has asserted as a determination of the importance of the testimony. I think the importance of this testimony and the -- was apparent during the course of the trial, is apparent here, and whether or not the Prosecution seeks to permit the witness to -- or ask the Appellate Chamber to go further with this is an entirely different matter. So I don't want this to be accepted in any way, shape, or form in the manner characterised by the -- by the Defence counsel. In any event, Your Honours, I note the time. I indicated I would have one question before the break, and I'm at the Appellate Chamber's disposal.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE POCAR
utterances.text: Well, it's probably appropriate now to make the break, and we reconvene in 20 minutes. The hearing is adjourned.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE POCAR
utterances.text: We resume the hearing, and I give the floor to the Prosecution --

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE POCAR
utterances.text: -- to continue his questioning. Please.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Mr. Karadzic, before we adjourned for the recess we were looking at that portion of your statement where you asserted that the strategic goals were political and not military. I have turned your attention to a couple of comments. Let me turn you next to the army's view, and I want to direct your attention to P529, tab 255, which is the analysis of the combat readiness and activities of the army of Republika Srpska in 1992, a document labelled military secret, strictly confidential, and produced in April of 1993, a retrospect. Page 159 in English of that document, and the Trial Chamber heard evidence of this, said that: "The strategic objectives of our war which were promptly defined and set before the Main Staff of the army of Republika Srpska, the commands and units served as a general guideline upon which we planned the actual operations and concerted battles." And it goes on on the next page to note that priorities and discharging set or approved tasks were selected depending on the actual stages of the war. It indicates that thus the primary focus for the army of Republika Srpska for quite some time had been to open and maintain a corridor linking the Republic of Serbian Krajina through the Bosnian Krajina with Serbia. And then it continues: "In the last month and a half, our operations have concentrated on the liberation of Podrinje as, thereby, the strategic objective of war would be realised, one that could be defined as establishing -- as establishing contact with Serbia on the River Drina or the Drina ceasing to be a frontier." Mr. Karadzic that's strategic objective number 3, isn't it, the Drina ceasing to be a border?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN KARADZIC
utterances.text: First of all, that's not the case, and I'd like to tell you to look at the transcript of the 12th of May session where I said that the Drina was not to be the border between two worlds, the Catholic world and the Islamic Orthodox world. And in a television interview in 1993, and you have that interview here, I explain what I mean by that, that it will be a soft European border without any restrictions at the border. And I go on to say that Europe will go on softening its borders, and I say that Mr. Izetbegovic said that the Serbs would not need a passport at the Drina River. So if we want to look at the whole truth you have to look at the context. It is the context of the conference of Bosnia-Herzegovina. The European Union offered up a state unit to us, an entity, a republic in Bosnia-Herzegovina, and everything that was going on and going to happen should be looked at within that context. We never gave up on the Lisbon paper, and at the end of August 1992, the Lisbon document was replaced by Vance-Owen, then Stoltenberg and the Contact Group and finally Dayton. So you can't view this isolated, and as I say, look at what I said on the 12th of May, 1992. Take a look at that. I said that there should not be a border between two worlds because the Drina River was conceived as a border between two worlds, the eastern and western Christianity and Islam. And I wanted to advocate that it should not be a border between two worlds and not a border between Serbia and Bosnia, and that's what I said at the session. And in 1993, in the interview, I said it should be a soft border, not that there should be no border but that it should be a border without restrictions, and I quoted the EU and that it would make borders, its own borders soft and permeable. I don't know when Schengen existed at that time, but anyway, I envisaged that that's what Europe was going to tend towards and that we wanted to do the same because we wanted Bosnia to be the Switzerland of the Balkans, that it should be cantonised so that we could live in peace. And if you take individual parts out of context then you get a different meaning, but in order to view the whole we have to see the context in which that was said.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: We'll leave it then to the Chamber to decide whether or not that's the -- that is an articulation of strategic goal number 3 since I didn't hear a direct answer to that question. But let me note page 159 of the combat readiness report in talking about the strategic objectives of the war which were promptly set before the Main Staff. It continued: "This means that objectives were set before us rather than specific tasks spelled out, although the president of the republic as the supreme commander of the armed forces of RS did orally assign a number of tasks which were of general and vital significance to our struggle in protecting the Serbian people and its territories." The Main Staff of the army of RS translated the set objectives and tasks into general and individual missions with the goals of each -- of every individual combat operation, it says, at some point being defined. Similarly, on page 153 of this document which appears right above your name as Supreme Commander of the armed forces of Republika Srpska, Dr. Karadzic, it says: "This relationship between the command structures and the organs of government and the supreme command made it impossible for the Main Staff to make decisions absolutely on its own, rather every operational battle was politically endorsed on the basis of the interests of the Serbian people and approved by the highest authorities of Republika Srpska." But you have said, Dr. Karadzic, some aspect of the ways in which the political -- the strategic objectives were pursued politically, and no one is asserting that there wasn't an effort, a simultaneous effort, to pursue the strategic objectives politically as well as militarily, and in that connection let's look at what General Mladic said at the 34th session of the Bosnian Serb Assembly in 1993.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBINSON
utterances.text: Excuse me. Excuse me, Mr. President. If I can make an intervention. I'm not sure I understand what Mr. Tieger is doing. He is reading from documents without putting a question to the witness. He's making a long intervention about what some documents say as if he's making his closing submissions to you but not putting any question to the witness, so I think that's unfair to Dr. Karadzic to be simply commenting, which is not Mr. Tieger's role in these proceedings. So I would ask that either he refrain from commenting on the testimony and ask a question or that he -- when he does ask a question he tie it to the material that he's trying to introduce. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Well, Your Honour, it was my intention to wrap it up into one question but I'll be happy to break it into two.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Mr. Karadzic, I just read you from the combat readiness report which indicated that the political leadership was aware of all the operational battles, including those which sought to pursue the strategic objectives of the war which were, as we noted earlier, the corridor linking the Republic of Serbian Krajina through Bosnian Krajina and the elimination of the Drina as a border. That's the case, isn't it, Mr. Karadzic, that you were well aware of and that the Bosnian Serb leadership was aware of the pursuit of the strategic goals through the operations of the VRS?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN KARADZIC
utterances.text: That's not how it was, not Serbian Krajina. That's the right, Mr. Tieger. This is how it was: If you look at Cutileiro's maps, the ones we received in a package of proposals by the European Community for resolving the problem in Bosnia-Herzegovina, you'll see that those strategic goals are figured -- figure into that, and we know that many people consider that our army should liberate the whole of Bosnia and lead to a political solution that way. We said that cannot be. We said it must be the solution accepted and put forward by the European Community, not a solution that would hold the whole of Bosnia and Herzegovina within the frameworks of Yugoslavia. And there were opinions like that, you needn't think there weren't, that Bosnia-Herzegovina should be held in Yugoslavia and that Bosnia-Herzegovina step down from Yugoslavia unlawfully. So in that sense those goals were important, for example, that the army could not cross over onto the left bank the Una River and liberate Cazinska Krajina over there, which was 90 per cent Muslim, and according to Cutileiro's plan was envisaged to be a Muslim republic. So that was why it was important for the army to be aware of what the negotiations were about and what was happening at the conference to deal with the crisis in Bosnia-Herzegovina. They're not goals that we thought up or imagined or imposed on the army. It is information to the army as to what it should not do. And as far as communication is concerned, before the war broke out it wasn't necessary, you know, for all three republics to have territorial continuity. The Sasina Krajina was envisaged not to have continuity with Central Bosnia, not to follow on from Central Bosnia where there was a Muslim republic, but once you had a war in May in Banja Luka, 12 babies died because we no oxygen to give them, for the babies in the incubators to be saved. So if you had a war on your hands and we said that to Izetbegovic, if it is a war solution, then that's another matter entirely. But we were always in favour of a political solution and the proposal made by the European Commission was acceptable to us, although we had to make a very painful compromise not to be in Yugoslavia any more, and in essence, the army had to know what was envisaged by the Lisbon Agreement and that's the crux of the matter.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Well, in connection with the question of whether the political goals were pursued militarily and whether the army was aware of the political goals and acted upon them, I indicated we'd look at General Mladic at 529, tab 436, at the 34th session, and he said: "First, the people in the army with the help from the rest of us according to our possibilities have carried out most of the tasks and strategic goals set to them. We have created Republika Srpska." And he continued on the next page after discussing negotiations and said: "I have to say to our delegation, which I really appreciate together with our president, Mr. President, you have started from the most favourable starting position in Geneva. You had the military result in your hands. You and the people and the army and the forces of MUP have created it." And that was General Mladic talking about the military implementation of the strategic goals, wasn't it?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN KARADZIC
utterances.text: Well, you see, certainly the army wanted to have its merits recognised just as the political leadership liked to have its merits recognised for what was going on, but we were promised a republic by the European Community, and within the frameworks of the Cutileiro Plan or, rather, within the frameworks of the conference of Yugoslavia canton Cutileiro, and what we achieved is what we were given and promised and which we accepted as a replacement for stepping down from Yugoslavia. So if the army defended what we received as a proposal from the European Commission and accepted, on the 18th of March all three sides accepted the Lisbon Agreement, and everything that happened from the new year onwards and in February, March, April, and so on, all that was in -- within the context of the conference in Bosnia-Herzegovina, and I saw enormous mistakes being made when you look at sentences isolated and when you forget that an agreement was reached on the 18th of May, a solution to avoid war and one which was very similar to the Dayton Agreement which ended the war. So that is the substance.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ...

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN KARADZIC
utterances.text: It's not that we came up with that solution.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Let's look at, then, how the army pursued and achieved what you felt the Bosnian Serbs had been promised, and in that connection I'd like to look at P892, tab 12. That's directive number 4. This is dated November 19, 1992, another strictly confidential document, directive for further operations of the army of Republika Srpska.
