It notes on page 3 that some of the tasks from directive number 3 hadn't been carried out and that although the Posavina corridor had been substantially widened, the Hercegovina Corps had failed to reach the left bank of the Neretva and secure access to the sea. But then on page 5 it gives this direction to the Drina Corps: "From its present positions its main forces shall persistently defend Visegrad, the dam, Zvornik and the corridor, while the rest of its forces in the wider Podrinje region shall exhaust the enemy, inflict the heaviest possible losses on him and force him to leave the Birac, Zepa and Gorazde areas together with the Muslim population."

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBINSON
utterances.text: Excuse me, Mr. President. I'm going to object to any questions with respect to this directive. First I ask you to exempt Mr. Karadzic from answering the question on Rule 90(H). We're very far afield from Mr. Krajisnik and the strategic goals. Secondly, if you believe that there is some relevance to this question, we would ask under Article 21(4)(g) and Rule 90(E) that he be exempted from answering unless the Prosecution is willing to agree that the answer would not be used in his own trial, which, frankly, seems to be the primary purpose for these questions.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Your Honour, let me ask one question -- I will respond but let me ask one question first to see how far afield we are from the strategic goals and Mr. Krajisnik.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Mr. Karadzic, in 34th session that I mentioned where General Mladic made the remarks that I referred to about how the army had created Republika Srpska and achieved the goals and given the military result, at that session you spoke early in the session and enumerated the strategic goals at length, and then later on in the session Mr. Karadzic -- excuse me, Mr. Krajisnik spoke and once again enumerated and explained the strategic goals. Isn't correct?

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBINSON
utterances.text: Again, Mr. President, I'm going to make the same objection that just -- particularly with respect to Article 21(4)(g) and Rule 90(E) and ask that he be exempted from giving that answer.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE POCAR
utterances.text: As I see the question, the second part of it, could be answered, when Mr. Tieger asked whether Mr. Krajisnik enumerated and explained the strategic goals. From the first part certainly Mr. Karadzic can be exempt but the second goes to the act of and the conduct of Mr. Krajisnik. So please, Mr. Karadzic, you can answer the second part of it. That is whether Mr. Krajisnik spoke on that meeting and enumerated and explained the strategic goals.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] First of all, in order for the full truth to come out I have to say that it is quite natural for the political and the military aspect to compete as to who created the Republika Srpska. The Republika Srpska was not created by the army, because up until the end of 1992 there was not the structure. It was created only on the 20th of May. The military did not have its structure. Republika Srpska was created at the time when it was offered to us by the European Commission in political terms, and the military defended what was offered to us. If Krajisnik -- well, I don't know if Krajisnik commented on that, but those were legitimate political goals to retain what we had achieved at the Lisbon conference. So it is quite possible for him to have commented, but this was not a secret document. It was the political goal that the army defended, and it is quite natural for the officers to like to ascribe some credit to themselves, but this was a political goal and Republika Srpska was created before we had the army.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE POCAR
utterances.text: Mr. Karadzic, you were asked whether Krajisnik spoke on that meeting and explained the strategic goals, and you answered that it was possible that he did. That means that -- that you don't know whether he did or not? Is that --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I don't. I don't know whether he did. Yes, that is my response. I can't see the document in front of me. I don't know the minutes. But anybody could talk about the strategic goals because those were not a secret document. That was a political platform for our negotiations with the European Community.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE POCAR
utterances.text: I thank you. I wanted just to have a precise answer. Mr. Tieger.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Mr. Krajisnik participated with you in the formulation of those strategic goals, didn't he?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN KARADZIC
utterances.text: I don't recall that, but the whole Assembly participated in this effort. I think that during the break there was a commission, about ten people, who helped me formulate it, and when I went out to speak, to address the Assembly, the original strategic goals can be found in the transcript from that session of the Assembly.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Mr. Karadzic, in the short amount of time I have remaining, I just want to conclude this portion of the examination in which we're addressing both the implementation of the strategic goals and your assertion that there was no policy of ethnic separation, and in that connection I want to turn to P865, an order of May 28th by Major Svetozar Andric. That document which the Trial Chamber saw, Mr. Karadzic, indicates as following: "The moving out of the Muslim population must be organised and coordinated with the municipalities through which the moving is carried out. Only women and children can move out while men fit for military service are to be placed in camps for exchange." And before I ask my question let me also turn your attention to P892, tab 90. That's a document from the 1st Krajina Corps command on the 14th of June, 1992, and it indicates: "The most difficult situation concerns the Muslim and Croat refugees in the area of Autonomous Region Krajina. Their security and the provision of food. The attempt to expel them to Central Bosnian failed because of transportation difficulties and their resistance to leaving their places of residence." Now, those are two reflections of how the military result and the attainment of the strategic objectives through the efforts of the VRS and the MUP were implemented. Isn't that correct, Dr. Karadzic?

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBINSON
utterances.text: Excuse me, Mr. President. I'm going to invoke Rule 90(E) and Article 21(4)(g) as to this answer. That's a matter that's properly for Mr. Karadzic's trial, not Mr. Krajisnik's proceedings. But if they would like an answer to that question, they can apply for an order guaranteeing that it not be used against him and he'll be happy to and answer the question. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Your Honour, this witness has come forward before this Trial Chamber, put a statement before the Trial Chamber which Mr. Krajisnik asked it to rely upon which puts all of these matters at issue. He's certainly within his right to refuse to answer, but our position is that bears completely on the credibility of the statement. Our position on the credibility of this witness is clear, and we leave it to the Appeals Chamber to assess. I just have two more questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE POCAR
utterances.text: You have exhausted your time, but I'm ready to give you five or ten minutes to conclude your --

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE POCAR
utterances.text: -- questioning.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: I may -- I may -- I will do that and I'll try to do that as quickly as possible.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Mr. Karadzic, I want to turn your attention to two more documents; the first is P447. That's a report on some aspects of the work done to date and the tasks ahead on 17 July 1992 from the minister of the interior, sent to the president of the Presidency, that was you, and to the Prime Minister. And in that report the minister details some of the issues which restrict the MUP members of some of the other tasks within their purview, complains about some of the burdens that the MUP members are -- are facing, and he writes: "The army Crisis Staffs and War Presidencies have requested that the army round up or capture as many Muslim civilians as possible, and they leave such undefined camps to internal affairs organs. The conditions in some of these camps are poor. There is no food. Individuals sometimes do not observe international norms, et cetera." Then he goes on to say that there's a shortage -- shortage of personnel is also a limiting factor as he continues to detail some of the burdens faced by the MUP including the detention of all these Muslim civilians. Now, that roundup of Muslim civilians by the army, the Crisis Staffs, and the War Presidencies, Dr. Karadzic, is another reflection of the manner in which the objectives of the Bosnian Serb leadership as put to the army were implemented. Isn't that right?

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. President. Again I'm going to make the same objection. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE POCAR
utterances.text: Okay. I take note of that. Mr. Tieger, your last question.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Last document, Mr. Karadzic. That's P1160. This is a combat report, and it says: "During the day the village of Novoseoci was ciscenje," that is cleansed or mopped up, "in Glasinacko Polje." Now, the Trial Chamber heard evidence in the case, Mr. Karadzic, that the ciscenje, the cleansing, of Novoseoci was accomplished by separating the men from the women and executing the men. And the author of this report is Lieutenant Colonel Radislav Krstic, in 1992. Is it correct, Mr. Karadzic, that Mr. -- that Colonel Krstic continued in the service of the VRS after his ciscenje activities in Eastern Bosnia?

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBINSON
utterances.text: Really, Mr. President, I again think this is so far afield from what you are supposed to be interested in in this hearing. It is nothing more than a transparent attempt to use his answers against him at his own trial, and I would ask that he be exempted from answering that question or any questions like that under Rule 90(E) and Article 21(4)(g). Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Counsel can continue to persist in -- he's more than welcome, of course, to invoke his client's rights but his assertion that this is far afield from a statement in which this witness asks the Appellate Chamber to believe his assertion that there was no policy of ethnic separation is, in my submission, wholly unfounded. In light of the invocation of -- this witness's invocation of his rights, Your Honour, I will conclude my examination and thank the Appellate Chamber for the time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE POCAR
utterances.text: Thank you. The Chamber will consider how far it is from the -- from the purpose of this examination, of this hearing, and takes note of the -- of the invocation of the right of the -- of the witness. So this concludes the examination by the Prosecution, and now we -- the Judges want to put some questions to the witness; they're allowed to do so. Judge Shahabuddeen, Judge Guney, and then Judge Meron.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SHAHABUDDEEN
utterances.text: Dr. Karadzic --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, please, for the Judge.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SHAHABUDDEEN
utterances.text: I'm not in command of the technology. Dr. Karadzic, I would value your help in resolving a small question of credibility. It concerns the old question whether or not Mr. Krajisnik was a member of the Presidency. Now, you have said, so I gather, that the Presidency only came into being after a declaration of war. Do you remember saying so?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN KARADZIC
utterances.text: I said that the Presidency would have existed had a state of war been declared, but a state of war was not declared.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SHAHABUDDEEN
utterances.text: Now, do you mean by that reference a formal declaration of a state of war?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN KARADZIC
utterances.text: Yes. In legal terms this means that a whole set of laws have to be in place and there is a procedure for the state government when the state of war is declared laws are no longer in application, and a different set of regulations then apply for the state of war. That doesn't mean that the low intensity conflict that existed, not in our territory, but in areas adjacent to -- areas controlled by the other ethnic communities, it doesn't mean that there wasn't combat, but a state of war, which means that some stipulations in the constitutions are suspended and that new laws have to be declared, well, this was not done. The state of war was not declared.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SHAHABUDDEEN
utterances.text: You are aware, sir, that nations do, in practice, go to war without there being a formal declaration of war.

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN KARADZIC
utterances.text: We wanted to retain the civilian quality of life throughout the conflict, because we were hoping that a political solution would be found any time, because the conference was going on at all times. The talks, the conference about the political solution were ongoing, and that's why we did not want to introduce wartime laws and wartime lifestyle and regime.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SHAHABUDDEEN
utterances.text: Now, the Presidency would have involved main features of the constitution of your state. Now, would your secretaries be expected to be familiar with the main features of the principle elements of your state such as the Presidency?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN KARADZIC
utterances.text: Well, you're entirely right when it comes to the secretary of the Presidency. It's a political function. But when we're talking about the typists, the secretaries who just take notes or serve the Presidency, they did not have to know those things, and they couldn't know that because this was not an area of their expertise. But my chief of office, the Secretary-General of the Presidency, they were lawyers and they would have known that, but they did not attend those sessions, and they did not keep notes or minutes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SHAHABUDDEEN
utterances.text: Now, did you or any of your principal officers, to your knowledge, ever speak with the secretaries about their imprecision in treating Mr. Krajisnik as if he were a member of the Presidency?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN KARADZIC
utterances.text: Well, we did not have any need to talk to them in this way because we did not consider the minutes to be an important document. Minutes could be as imprecise as they were. It was just an aide-memoire about the things that were discussed, and then on the basis of the minutes, my secretaries and my assistants made decisions that then I signed. The minutes themselves were not important. If you allow me to explain why Mr. -- why the Prime Minister and president of the Assembly participated or attended. In normal circumstances, I would write a memo to the government and to the assembly, and I would give them 15 days to inform me how this initiative or an initiative of the Presidency could be implemented, whether the government was already doing something about that, whether there was anything ongoing in the Assembly on the topic that I raised. And since I did not have the 15 days, I didn't have the time to write to them and then wait for their response, I invited them to attend the session of the Presidency in order for them to be able to tell me whether there were any such initiatives in the Assembly, whether the government was able to actually implement it. That is why they attended. Some ministers also attended and this did not make them members of the Presidency.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SHAHABUDDEEN
utterances.text: Thank you, sir.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE POCAR
utterances.text: Judge Vaz, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE VAZ
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. President. Mr. Karadzic, you've just told us that you did not have time to send documents 15 days in advance in order to get feedback, response from the relevant authorities and that this was the reason why you were under an obligation to invite them to the sessions. Do I have to understand this in this manner, that you expected those persons to present their opinions at the sessions and not just be there to follow the developments since after that you were able to send to them the minutes which would serve to inform them, since they did not play any role at the sessions?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN KARADZIC
utterances.text: In the decision-making process, since all three of us members of the Presidency were professionals in other areas of expertise, Mr. Koljevic was a Shakespearologist, I am a doctor myself, and Mrs. Plavsic is a biologist, we tried not to make any mistakes in the decision-making process, and we needed to know first of all whether any decisions had already been made on this topic, whether it -- the procedure was on-going in the government or in the Assembly, and we wanted to hear from the government whether this decision could be implemented, whether it was legal and reasonable. So in this decision-making process we needed input from the two bodies because we're talking about the three major institutions: The Presidency, the Assembly, and the government. The president of the Assembly is not an institution, as you know, it's the speaker of the Assembly, but we needed to know what legislation -- he needed to know what legislation he would receive in the Assembly. The president of the government, the Prime Minister, would be able to tell us whether this was all in accordance with the law and whether this could be implemented. This is why they attended the sessions of the Presidency.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE VAZ
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you very much. You also said that these minutes that were sent after the sessions could be documents that would be signed by your lady secretary. In view of the fact that you primarily signed these minutes, should one believe that your signature on these minutes did not really attach any value to them?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN KARADZIC
utterances.text: Well, no value was attached to them because we even have a particular post, a note-taker, a note-taking clerk. Anybody could be that. This is just an aide-memoire as to what was stated at a session so that on the basis of that I could formulate a decision or an order and send it further on to those who are to be the recipients. These minutes have no importance whatsoever. Even Mr. Kupresanin was mentioned here, he is a of a different party, not a member of the SDS, but he is head of the patriotic front. According to our system, a member of parliament can say whatever he wishes and will not be held responsible. It's not the position of the government. There is unlimited freedom of speech and freedom as such on the part of MPs. It is the decisions that carry weight, proper documents coming from the Presidency. But these minutes that come from Presidency meetings when we would call a session within 15 minutes or so when the government or somebody asked us for a decision, we would meet within 15 minutes, we'd ask Krajisnik and Djeric to come and to inform us as to whether we can make such a decision. It's the decisions that are important, that matter. A note is just a note.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE VAZ
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. Karadzic, and thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE POCAR
utterances.text: Judge Guney, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE GUNEY
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. Mr. Karadzic, in the summary of the written statement relating to the finding in paragraph 1121 as to Krajisnik and Serbian Democratic Party, you said then Krajisnik was not your candidate for the post of the president of the parliament and his nomination was the result of bargain. Could you tell us who were the participants to such bargain, and you personally, did you took part in such bargain? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN KARADZIC
utterances.text: Immediately after the elections, having seen that the political scene was a heated one and in the social atmosphere as such, I came up with a proposal to establish an expert government. The other two sides did not admit that, but I did carry that through. That is to say, within this joint government of Bosnia and Herzegovina, among all our ministers and deputy ministers only one minister was a member of the SDS. All the rest were experts. I wanted the president of the parliament to be someone who was not within the party although he was on our list. That was Mr. Trbojevic. And I asked a lady journalist, a Muslim with a European orientation to sound this out, to see how that would be received if Mr. Trbojevic were to be president the parliament. She checked that out. She did the sounding and said that that would be received well among the Muslims in Sarajevo. And I made that proposal. However, there were two important objections that were made to me by the personnel commission of the Executive Committee. First of all that we handed over all the power we won in the elections to experts and non-party persons; and secondly, that I even wanted to give the position of president of parliament to someone who was not a member of the SDS. And thirdly, from the Banja Luka Krajina there was a complaint that there were no people from Krajina. The word "people from Krajina" is "krajisnik" in Serbian literally. So then I had to either change the list of ministers or I had to accept that the president of parliament had to be a person from the party and from the Krajina, and then I said something by way of a joke. Somebody had made a suggestion to me and I knew Krajisnik very well and we were friends, too, and then I said, "Very well, you will have krajisnik." And I asked Mr. Krajisnik to come and Mr. Ostojic didn't even recognise him. He didn't even let him in. He didn't even know why we were calling in a Krajisnik. Then I had to ask for Mr. Krajisnik to be brought in again. When I nominated him, then the MPs from Krajina laughed and said, "You turn out to be smarter than us," because I said you would have krajisnik. His last name means that he comes from Krajina, and he feels that he does hail from Krajina because that is where he hails from originally. So that is the essence of how the choice was Mr. Krajisnik. He was the sixth person on the list. 0.25 per cent was the margin by which he got into parliament. Otherwise, he would not have even gotten into parliament as such. One did not count on him to be the president of the parliament.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE GUNEY
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Karadzic. Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE POCAR
utterances.text: I turn to Judge Meron.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MERON
utterances.text: Dr. Karadzic, I have two or three questions to ask you. The first one pertains to the conclusion made by the Trial Chamber that the record of the Presidency of 9 October 1992 was signed by Mr. Krajisnik as chairman. Now, you claim in your statement that these minutes are in error and that the minutes of the real Presidency session were not signed by Mr. Krajisnik. So I have two questions to ask you here. First, how do you account for the existence of these minutes which you describe as false? And secondly, have you ever tried to issue a corrigendum, as we would expect any institution to issue, if the original minutes were not correct? If there is no record of such a corrigendum, why would you want us to believe that those records actually signed by Mr. Krajisnik were not correct?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN KARADZIC
utterances.text: Well, this is the way it is: This could not have been a session of the Presidency. They met -- I mean, out of us members of the Presidency it was only Mrs. Plavsic that attended. Mr. Koljevic and I were supposed to arrive. However, since we hadn't arrived, as they were awaiting us they had a discussion. This was a free discussion. Not a single decision was made, not a single conclusion was made, nothing that would be a document pertaining to the remit of the Presidency. The secretary composed a note on this, expecting us to come. Since we did not show up then this was given to someone to sign so that we -- there would be some kind of a record of what it was that they were discussing. This was a conversation not a meeting of the Presidency, and I could not draw any document out of that that they had discussed. These were recommendations, thoughts, and so on. This was not a session of the Presidency. On the basis of that, I could not -- on the basis of these minutes or whatever, the fact that they met up and talk, I could not base any decision of the Presidency on that because there was no meeting with the Presidency. This was an internal note. As I've said already, our minutes were viewed in that sense, as internal notes about what was discussed and also as an aide-memoire in order to be able to reach a decision, I or some other member of the Presidency to draft a decision and sign a decision on the basis of that. Just look at the minutes that are being discussed and you will see that nothing was concluded there. Nothing was adopted there. It's quite simple that two other members of the Presidency were being awaited and people were discussing things in the meantime.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MERON
utterances.text: Dr. Karadzic, I did not ask you so much about the content of that meeting and the significance of the decisions. My question pertained to the fact that Mr. Krajisnik signed as a chairman, and even that did not -- you did not sense that this was correct -- was incorrect and it needed to be corrected by a corrigendum?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN KARADZIC
utterances.text: Well, you see, as I keep saying, I did not consider the minutes to be a document, an enactment. Quite simply it's an aide-memoire, a reminder. I didn't think it was necessary, because we had to discuss all of this yet again when the full composition of the Presidency was there. For me this was just a note, and it was of no relevance.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MERON
utterances.text: Thank you. Then I would like to turn to this question, Dr. Karadzic: The Trial Chamber found that in terms of power and influence, and I'm quoting, you were number one, the numero uno and that Mr. Krajisnik was the number two of the regime. Yet in your statement which you -- which we are discussing today you assert that Mr. Krajisnik exerted very little power in government. So my question to you: Could you please describe for us, for the Appeals Chamber, what was actually Mr. Krajisnik's role and authority in the government?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN KARADZIC
utterances.text: Mr. Krajisnik had had no powers whatsoever within the government. Even if you look at the word "cabinet" as such, if you look at the minutes you will see that he never attended the sessions, and his proposals never got there, or some documents from him. The cabinet, the government, was fully independent in its functioning and particularly it was independent of the president of the parliament. The Presidency and the parliament and the government were our institutions, not the president of the parliament. He was no institution. Mr. Krajisnik did enjoy a reputation. You cannot deny that. He actually won this reputation in the parliament with the Muslims and the Croats because he was very skilful, very conciliatory in manner, and this was watched on TV as a drama and that's how he got this reputation, but he didn't really have any powers or authority whatsoever. He had the authority to prepare a session of parliament and if someone had something to do, and primarily it was the ministries that were supposed to do that although a group of MPs would have the right to propose a bill and the Presidency would have the right to process a bill, then Mr. Krajisnik was supposed to put that into parliamentary procedure and to carry this out the way he did in the joint Assembly, skilfully, in a conciliatory manner once -- until a decision was reached where there would be no out-voting. We agreed that we should like to have unanimous decisions or nearly unanimous decisions. That also happened in the joint Assembly with the Croats and the Muslims except for some questions that had to do with our absolute fate, the destiny of Yugoslavia. Thanks to the skill of Mr. Krajisnik, agreement was reached to a large degree on many questions and they did not contribute to decisions. As for the government, please take a look at this. Somebody can look at the minutes of government sessions. I or Mr. Krajisnik did not meddle in the work of the government. I believe that I was not number one. It was the Assembly that was number one, not Mr. Krajisnik. Number two was probably the Presidency and number three was the government. However, as an institution, as an institution not as individuals.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MERON
utterances.text: Finally, Dr. Karadzic, I would like to ask you a very specific question about the appointment of Ratko Mladic. In your statement, you discuss that on page 10, you discuss your own involvement, and the Trial Chamber dealt with this in paragraph 994 of its judgement, concluding that Ratko Mladic was selected jointly by yourself and by Mr. Krajisnik. Could you describe to us Mr. Krajisnik's role in the appointment of Ratko Mladic?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN KARADZIC
utterances.text: He had no role whatsoever. He could only put this to a vote. According to the constitution when I was elected to the Presidency, the Presidency had the authority to nominate the chief of the Main Staff. Up until the 12th of May we had only two members of the Presidency that were equal. Neither of the two chaired the Presidency. This was Mrs. Plavsic and Mr. Kraljevic. You see, for example, in April when this two-person Presidency consisting of the two of them makes a decision, say, on stopping the shelling of Sarajevo, it's the Prime Minister who turns that decision into an order because there is to Presidency yet. When I was elected member of the Presidency and president of the Presidency, I could nominate Mr. Mladic. However, I let parliament do that because I had just acceded to this position. Now, how was the proposal made? Mr. Krajisnik had nothing whatsoever to do with that. Two high-ranking officers of the former Yugoslav People's Army came to me and they said if at the conference in Lisbon you got the right to a National Guard or to an army of your own then our recommendation to you would be to take an officer from Bosnia-Herzegovina. In particular, we would like to recommend one officer and that is Ratko Mladic. And I asked around a bit about Ratko Mladic and I heard that he was a decent officer, strict, of high morale -- morality, resolute. I had never seen him before, and then I formulated that proposal. No one else had anything to do with the proposal. As for the nomination, all the MPs accepted my proposal that it would be Mladic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MERON
utterances.text: So you deny that Mr. -- you're denying that Mr. Krajisnik had any role to play in the appointment of Mr. Mladic?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN KARADZIC
utterances.text: Absolutely. These two officers who made the proposal to me can testify to the fact that there was no one else there but me when they made that proposal to me. Although I don't consider that to be a crime, but the truth is the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MERON
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE POCAR
utterances.text: I thank you. I believe we can now start the re-examination of Dr. Karadzic by the Defence. I turn to the Defence, either Mr. Krajisnik or Mr. Dershowitz, bearing in mind that this is a re-examination and not an examination-in-chief. I want to warn as of now that the re-examination has to go to what has been raised in cross-examination. MR. N. DERSHOWITZ: May I have one moment to consult --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE POCAR
utterances.text: Yes. MR. N. DERSHOWITZ: -- to see how we're going to divide the time?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE POCAR
utterances.text: Sure. MR. N. DERSHOWITZ: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE POCAR
utterances.text: MR. N. DERSHOWITZ: If I may, Mr. Krajisnik has indicated he'd like to take 10 minutes and then turn over the remaining time to me. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE POCAR
utterances.text: That's fine. So then, Mr. Krajisnik, you have the floor.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRAJISNIK
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Karadzic, the minutes were mentioned today of the 9th of October, 1992. I signed it as the presiding person. Now, I'm going to ask you, there's a decision here on the appointment of an advisor to the Presidency, Mr. Djukanovic, and the evidentiary number is 02298631, the reference number, and this was passed on the 9th of October, 1992. That means that if these minutes are true and correct, this decision should be contained in those minutes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ...

utterances.speaker: JUDGE POCAR
utterances.text: Sorry, Mr. Tieger?

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: I think the Chamber will rarely hear a more leading question. I would ask the questions to be -- of the witness called by Mr. Krajisnik to be fairly open and not suggest the answer to the witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE POCAR
utterances.text: Well, go on, Mr. Krajisnik.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRAJISNIK
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Tieger is an old acquaintance of mine and he is trying to mislead the client as he did -- trip up the client as he did earlier on. Here, gentlemen, you have the decision passed at that session just for Mr. Karadzic to confirm whether it was brought in at that session or not, that I signed or not. If it wasn't, then there -- that means there was another session and that the minutes are not in fact the minutes of the Presidency session. So that's my whole philosophy. So could Mr. Karadzic either confirm or deny that? Is the statement, this decision contained there or not?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN KARADZIC
utterances.text: May I go ahead and answer? This is a decision that we passed when Mr. Koljevic and I arrived with Mrs. Plavsic. So it was a Presidency meeting. That's when the two of us arrived. And it is the decision signed in my name by Mr. Koljevic with full authority. He had every right to do so, but the fact is that it was not incorporated into the part where there was a free discussion held before the quorum, that is to say, before the two of us arrived. I think that all of them had left when we made the decision that needed to be made because they were not able to make decisions because the three of us or, rather, the two of us weren't there. The quorum was not sitting in full. So this is an obvious example of that being the case and of Koljevic signing in my name.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRAJISNIK
utterances.text: Mr. Karadzic, can you be briefer? Shorter questions [as interpreted], please, and try and respect my time as you did the Prosecution's time? The minutes of the 13th of November, 1992, is what I'd like to look at next, which was quoted by the Prosecutor, which speaks quite precisely about whether a Presidency was established or whether it was suppose to be established in the future. Now, I'd like Mr. Karadzic to read out exactly the challenged portion which shows whether the Presidency existed at that time or whether it was supposed to be established at some time in the future.

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN KARADZIC
utterances.text: The Presidency considered the question of the justification of introducing a wartime commission and an expanded Presidency under the current conditions with respect to a parliamentary question. So it's the -- whether it was justified to introduce an expanded Presidency, that's the question. It was established that a state of war had not been declared for well-known reasons and that an expanded Presidency, including the president of the national assembly and the Prime Minister of Republika Srpska could be introduced only under such circumstances. The case is the same with the War Presidency which was introduced and replaced by the commission, in the municipalities that is. And then we have the law --

utterances.speaker: MR. KRAJISNIK
utterances.text: May we have your comments?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN KARADZIC
utterances.text: Well, I think the language here -- the fact that we're trying these cases in different languages gives rise to many problem. So perhaps the -- it's not ill-intent on the part of the Prosecution, but there is a confusion with respect to language. Now, as Mr. Tieger told me earlier on, what he read out I didn't recognise, but now we see it discussed the question of introducing a War Presidency, an expanded Presidency, the introduction of it. That's what was discussed. So it was not that it was introduced. The discussion was whether to introduce it or not and our decision was not to introduce it because there were no legal prerequisites for that.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRAJISNIK
utterances.text: Mr. Karadzic, the Prosecutor also mentioned the Assembly at which in Zvornik there was discussion about the same topic, that is to say, the Presidency was discussed there too. Now, the problem here is in the translation, gentlemen Judges. We can establish here that that is so, whether there were five members or three members. Now, I'm going to read it out, and would Mr. Karadzic like to confirm it or not. In the original text it says as follows, and Karadzic is speaking. It is page 59, the evidentiary number is 02149691, and it is the stenogram from the Assembly in Zvornik. And Karadzic says: "I always advocated the Presidency and not the president, because there are few of us as it is. If Koljevic and I go off somewhere, then Biljana remains. And at least there's one of us three there then. And then if Biljana has to leave, then Mr. Krajisnik." Now, I'd like to hear Mr. Karadzic's answer. From this text are we able to conclude who the Presidency members were?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN KARADZIC
utterances.text: It's quite clear that the members of the Presidency are myself, Mrs. Plavsic, and Mr. Nikola Koljevic. And I -- I never want to be the president of the republic but had to accept it in the end because the two of us [as interpreted] wanted it to be so and the proposal came from them. I was always reticent but I thought that it was difficult for one man to make those decisions, so I always relied on more people. However, here it is quite clear and it is stressed that the Presidency was us three, the three of us. If anyone of us was absent, then Biljana would be there. She can't make decisions but she can provide people with information. Now if Biljana wasn't there, then the information could be provided by Mr. Krajisnik too, but neither Ms. Plavsic or Mr. Krajisnik or myself could make decisions, or Mr. Koljevic themselves could make decisions on our own. So if Biljana was there and remained there, she could just provide information, just as anybody else could who knew what the discussions were about.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRAJISNIK
utterances.text: Mr. Karadzic, is it possible, and could the Prosecution help me out, could the combat report be provided to Mr. Karadzic that was presented here today where it says exactly what the strategic goals of the army were so that Mr. Karadzic could read that and then tell us whether they are the same strategic goals which were given on the 12th of May. So could the Prosecution help me out here, please. Mr. Tieger can read it out again if that is in order. Perhaps that would be best.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Two sections, Your Honour, on page 160. "Thus the primary focus for the army of Republika Srpska for quite some time had been to open and maintain a corridor linking the Republic of Serbian Krajina --"

utterances.speaker: MR. KRAJISNIK
utterances.text: [Interpretation] 159, page 159. Page 159 of the combat report you raised. The strategic goals are as follows, and then they were enumerated. That portion.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: "The strategic objectives of our war which were promptly defined and set before the Main Staff of the army of Republika Srpska. The commands and units served as a general guideline upon which we plan the actual operations and concerted battles. This means that objectives were set before --"

utterances.speaker: MR. KRAJISNIK
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Tieger, they were enumerated. The text isn't important, just the points one by one. Mr. Sladojevic will read it out if you can't find it, with the permission of the Appeals Chamber. Could Mr. Sladojevic read it out, by the Appeals Chamber's leave, because it's in English, and then I'll tell you exactly which document I'd like to refer to.

utterances.speaker: MR. SLADOJEVIC
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ... read it in English himself if Mr. Tieger gives him the document? That would be all right. Just the page 159, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE POCAR
utterances.text: Can you provide the witness with the document?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No. In no respect were those the goals that were declared as being the political goals. For example, look at the first one. The defence of the Serbian people against the genocide by the Muslim Croat forces. We make no mention of that anywhere because in the strategic goals of May we relied on the conference, that the conference would speedily bring in a political solution. And there was no discussion of any kind of defence at all at -- there. Furthermore, it says --

utterances.speaker: MR. KRAJISNIK
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KRAJISNIK
utterances.text: Mr. Karadzic, you can read it to yourself or read it out.

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN KARADZIC
utterances.text: [In English] "Against genocide at the hand of the Muslim Croat forces. The protection of the property and cultural heritage of the Serbian people, the liberation of the territories which are ours and which belong to us by historical birth rate -- birthright, the infliction of the greatest possible losses of the Muslim Croat forces to which end we have opted for neutralising and destroying their personnel and combat ordnance. The neutralising of all facilities in enemy territory or their destruction. The spreading of the enemy forces over a broad area on all battlefields of former Bosnia and Herzegovina." The gradual cross-erosion of the enemy's offensive power. Yes. That means the shattering of his forces and the seizing -- seizing of the initiative and creating conditions for resolute offensive operations in order to defeat his forces and expel them from areas that have always belonged to us while at the same time preventing massive losses in our own ranks. [Interpretation] This has absolutely nothing to do --

utterances.speaker: MR. KRAJISNIK
utterances.text: Mr. Karadzic, just a short question. Does this -- was there any possibility of linking up those strategic goals with the six strategic goals?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN KARADZIC
utterances.text: No. This has nothing to do with the six strategic goals.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRAJISNIK
utterances.text: My last question. Today the Prosecutor said -- or, rather, he showed you the minutes of the Presidency of the 2nd of August, and gentlemen Judges, it says there that three members of the Presidency informed the Presidency about the conference that was held on the 27th and 28th of July. Now, I should like to ask the Appeals Chamber -- or, rather, to draw attention to paragraph 306 of the Krajisnik appeal where a review was given or, rather, I quote two pieces of information. They were two pieces of information, two reports related to Mr. Karadzic's statement. So could he just read that out and then it will be quite clear that Mr. Karadzic addresses Mr. Krajisnik as president of the Assembly. That's his attitude towards him. And it's to be found in paragraph 306 of my appeal brief. One is a BBC piece of information and the other is from the Tanjug news agency.

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN KARADZIC
utterances.text: [In English] What would you like me -- [Interpretation] Would you like me to read it out?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE POCAR
utterances.text: What is your question, Mr. Krajisnik?

utterances.speaker: MR. KRAJISNIK
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KRAJISNIK
utterances.text: Yes. My question is this: Please read it out, and that is linked to the conference and the minutes that were presented in court today by Mr. Tieger.

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN KARADZIC
utterances.text: [In English] Yeah. Yeah. "The evidence -- the evidence the Chamber derived from Presidency minutes of August the 2nd, 1992, is erroneous as well. Here all three members of the delegation of negotiations in London are listed as member of the Presidency by mistake on the part of the person who took the minutes. Mr. Karadzic gave a statement to the BBC and Tanjug before his departure from the -- for the conference in London, 27th of July, 1992, stating that he and Koljevic were members of the Presidency and that Krajisnik was the president of the Assembly." That -- he was member of delegation in this capacity, not as a member of Presidency. That's what I say that the minutes -- minutes from some meetings are not documents.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRAJISNIK
utterances.text: Mr. Karadzic, thank you very much. I'll conclude my examination there. May we just have the document back, please? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRAJISNIK
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, thank you for giving me the opportunity to question Mr. Karadzic, and Mr. Dershowitz will continue.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE POCAR
utterances.text: Yes, please, Mr. Dershowitz. MR. N. DERSHOWITZ: Thank you very much, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. N
utterances.text: Mr. Karadzic, my name is Nathan Dershowitz, and I am what's called JCE counsel, and that is counsel with respect to the joint criminal enterprise, so I'd like to focus my questions to you with respect to Mr. Krajisnik's involvement and whether he was a member of a JCE, and because of the limited time, I would appreciate it if you could try to keep your answers short but accurate. Thank you. There have been a number of discussions of SDS, and I just want to know when SDS was first established, were there other political parties that had been established which were based largely on -- what were they based upon?

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Sorry, Your Honour. I'm not clear how that arises from the cross-examination. MR. N. DERSHOWITZ: Your Honour, I can make a proffer and that is I'm trying to establish -- there were questions with respect to SDS. I wanted to establish what SDS was. It's just a couple of preliminary questions in order to get to the specific questions which tie it in to the JCE.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE POCAR
utterances.text: Yes, but keep it short and -- MR. N. DERSHOWITZ: Three questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE POCAR
utterances.text: -- bear in mind the warning I gave you at the beginning. MR. N. DERSHOWITZ: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] We, a large group of Serb dissidents from the Communist days, refused to establish a political party on an ethnic basis. However, the SDA had already been established as the party of the Muslim people, and the HDZ spilled over from Croatia. It was established somewhat later, but it spilled over from Croatia, and it became clear that the Serb people had to have a party of their own or to vote for the Communists. That's what happened in Croatia. The Serbs voted for Racan's Communists and they did not fare well in the elections. MR. N. DERSHOWITZ:

utterances.speaker: MR. N
utterances.text: In the period 1990, 1991, did the SDS have an agenda, and what was the agenda?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN KARADZIC
utterances.text: Our plan and programme was highly complementary with the SDA programme. In their document of establishment, they said that they would not cooperate with parties that would work on the break-up of Yugoslavia. I had very good relations with Mr. Izetbegovic. We also saw each other privately, and he and I were both in favour of maintaining the federation, introducing democracy, replacing the Communist regime. So our plan was practically identical to that of the SDA. The HDZ had a somewhat different plan because they wanted Croatia and the Croat people, wherever they were, to leave Yugoslavia. The Muslims at that point, no. Mr. Izetbegovic, for as long as he was in favour of the Yugoslav option, the federal option, he enjoyed great support among the Serbs and Muslims in and out of parliament.

utterances.speaker: MR. N
utterances.text: Was it ever the agenda of SDA [sic] to "permanently remove by force or other means Bosnian Muslims and Bosnian Croats from large portions of Bosnia-Herzegovina through the commission of war crimes including murder, deportation, forced movement and inhumane acts"?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN KARADZIC
utterances.text: Now, I believe that you meant the SDS.

utterances.speaker: MR. N
utterances.text: Yes. I thought I said that. I think it's improperly transcribed.

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN KARADZIC
utterances.text: That was never the plan. There is an abundance of evidence showing that we wanted to -- for Bosnia to remain united. As a matter of fact, although we made plans that were supposed to save us from being out-voted but in the summer of 1991 when Mr. Zulfikarpasic and Filipovic came with a proposal of a historical agreement between the Muslims and the Serbs, we expressed our readiness to give up on all these pre-cautionary measures, to give up on regionalisation and to go back to the initial points of departure that the Serbs and Muslims had before the elections, that is to say, preserving Yugoslavia and preserving a single Bosnia-Herzegovina. When we had the conference not a single party had envisaged ethnically pure territories. Again I have to bring up the question of language. When somebody says purely Serbian, purely Muslim, purely Croat, it means undeniably Croat, Muslim or Serb. That created a great deal of confusion here in this Tribunal.

utterances.speaker: MR. N
utterances.text: Was Mr. Krajisnik involved in efforts prior to the outbreak of war to come up with a political solution?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN KARADZIC
utterances.text: Absolutely. Absolutely. He was highly conciliatory and he insisted until the very end on seeking a political solution.

utterances.speaker: MR. N
utterances.text: And prior to the outbreak of war, did you ever hear Mr. Krajisnik during the -- that period of time articulate his political views?

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: I object, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE POCAR
utterances.text: Mr. Dershowitz, you should you not proceed to an examination-in-chief. MR. N. DERSHOWITZ: It's not an examination-in-chief --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE POCAR
utterances.text: It is. MR. N. DERSHOWITZ: Okay. I'm sorry, Your Honour. I think there were some questions, with all due respect, about SDS and the SDS position. So what I am seeking to ask questions about, and there were numerous questions about SDS prior to the establishment, Your Honour, of the Presidency and the efforts were made to say that Mr. Krajisnik joined in those, so what I'm asking is his views as expressed at that time and whether he personally ever made any statements which would show that there was this guilt by association. We've heard a lot about the Serbian government or the Serbian representatives, and I'm asking questions following up as to whether Mr. Krajisnik ever made any of these comments prior to the establishment of the government. So with all due respect, they're followups to the specific questions that were asked.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE POCAR
utterances.text: Mr. Tieger.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: They might be followups if the underlying premise was correct. The only question that touched upon the SDS, there were questions directed at Variant A and B and that was it. There was no question about SDS activity prior to the war. MR. N. DERSHOWITZ: I'm sorry, some of the Judges did ask some questions with respect to SDS, and there were questions about the -- everything prior to the war which was -- were documents sent out by SDS? Was he an executive of SDS? Was the -- was there a distribution made by SDS? So what I'm looking for is a narrow question, a number of very narrow questions. I just want to know --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE POCAR
utterances.text: I want to avoid a long debate on this -- MR. N. DERSHOWITZ: I'm sorry.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE POCAR
utterances.text: -- but try to stick to the questions that were raised in cross-examination, please. MR. N. DERSHOWITZ:

utterances.speaker: MR. N
utterances.text: And my question to you is: Did you ever personally hear during any of the debates that took place prior to the establishment of the Presidency Mr. Krajisnik ever make any comments encouraging, advocating, suggesting ethnic cleansing, the movement of civilian populations, the murder of Muslims or Croats or any of these other war crimes that he's been charged with?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN KARADZIC
utterances.text: Absolutely not. It's not only that he was well known as a conciliatory person. He was also well known as a person who understood the Muslims. The Muslims themselves, Izetbegovic himself asked that Mr. Krajisnik always be on the negotiating team because they had a good understanding. So that was certainly not the case that anyone ever said any such thing. You're asking me about Mr. Krajisnik now. No one -- it never crossed anybody's mind, let alone did somebody ever say something like that.

utterances.speaker: MR. N
utterances.text: And prior to the outbreak of war, was Mr. Krajisnik in a position to issue orders as a member of SDS?

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Excuse me. I am sorry, Mr. Karadzic. This is not remotely raised by cross-examination. I certainly can't think of any questions by the Bench that would allow counsel to go into the direct examination that was covered by the 92 ter. MR. N. DERSHOWITZ: Your Honour, if I may respond, because I think that's just factually incorrect. There were a number of questions that were asked about distributions that were made by the Executive Board of SDS, that were made by the main office of SDS, and so the inference from the questions, which is what I am responding to, is that he as a member of Serbian leadership or SDS did certain things, and I want to ask the specific questions as to whether he personally would have issued any of these orders, why -- I'm only concerned about his personal responsibility, not as -- not the Serbian leadership. So my question is specifically responsive to the inference from those questions and the guilt by association. And so my narrow question is: Was he ever in a position to issue orders, directives, mandates in his capacity as a member of SDS? I see it's relevance.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE POCAR
utterances.text: Answer this question, Mr. Karadzic.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Absolutely not. He was not able to do that, nor did he do so. For a whole year of the existence of the SDS Mr. Krajisnik was not a member of the Main Board, and one year later at the annual Assembly when he was elected, he was already president of the joint Assembly and he was not in any other organ except in the Main Board where there were, I don't know how many, about a hundred or more people. I don't know how many members it had, but at any rate, he did not have a single function except one year later as a member of the Main Board, and as a member of the Main Board he could not issue any instructions, directives, or anything like that. MR. N. DERSHOWITZ:

utterances.speaker: MR. N
utterances.text: But was he actively involved in efforts to secure a peaceful resolution of the looming conflict?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN KARADZIC
utterances.text: Yes, but by virtue of his office of the president of the joint Assembly and also a member of the negotiating team first in the negotiations between Serbia, Croatia, Slovenia, and Bosnia and Macedonia, et cetera. Then when it turned out that the Bosnian delegation itself did not have a united position, then we turned within Bosnia-Herzegovina itself to see what the position of Bosnia would be. Again he held the office of this president of the joint Assembly, which he never left. Formally he was president of that Assembly until the end of 1992. It's only then that they replaced him, so no way was he anywhere on behalf of the SDS.

utterances.speaker: MR. N
utterances.text: I'd like to focus on the Presidency, and I must tell you that I am confused and I -- from some of the questions, I think there is confusion among the Bench so I'll try to clarify. I'd like to create three categories. Category number one is the Presidency, the formal Presidency. Category number two is the "expanded Presidency," a word frequently use, and category number three is the War Presidency. Okay? And my first question is with --

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: I'm sorry to interrupt. I'm having difficulty understanding how that -- where that distinction is based in fact and how it clarifies rather than further confuses. MR. N. DERSHOWITZ: If you would allow the witness to answer the questions maybe he can clarify it, but it is certainly confusing to me within the judgement and the questions.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: If the witness could be asked questions in an open manner rather than led to particular categories artificially created in advance that might help.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE POCAR
utterances.text: But there was a lot of discussion on the -- on how the Presidency was shaped, so I would -- I will be inclined to allow the Defence to clarify this issue, if it can be clarified. And since I have the floor, we're speaking of War Presidencies or War Commissioners? MR. N. DERSHOWITZ: Well, that's another one and --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE POCAR
utterances.text: Because I wanted to try to clarify that too. MR. N. DERSHOWITZ: And let me go one step further, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE POCAR
utterances.text: Okay. MR. N. DERSHOWITZ: And that's War Presidency or War Presidencies.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE POCAR
utterances.text: Okay. MR. N. DERSHOWITZ: All of which I think are in a state of confusion.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE POCAR
utterances.text: Go on. MR. N. DERSHOWITZ:

utterances.speaker: MR. N
utterances.text: With respect to the War Presidency -- I am sorry. Strike that. With respect to the Presidency, what are you referring to?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN KARADZIC
utterances.text: The Presidency of the Serb Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina up until the 12th of May was Biljana Plavsic and Nikola Koljevic, because they ran in the election and they were members of the joint Bosnia-Herzegovinian Presidency. I was elected on the 12th of May into the Presidency of -- this Presidency and I was elected president. So that was the collective head of state. Again we have a linguistic problem. Look at the first minutes from the session of the Presidency where it says "expanded session of the Presidency." Take a look at that. Often the SDS had expanded sessions. They were not sessions of the expanded board or committee. If I need to explain this further, the expanded --

utterances.speaker: MR. N
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ... some questions and maybe we can focus on this. Are you using the expression "Presidency" as the people who made decisions?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN KARADZIC
utterances.text: Yes, yes. That is the way the constitution defines it. It is subject matter from the constitution.

utterances.speaker: MR. N
utterances.text: So when you have meetings of the Presidency, you're talking about, when you were involved, the three people who were members of the Presidency who had the power to make decisions; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN KARADZIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. N
utterances.text: And when you're talking about the expanded Presidency or the expanded meetings of the Presidency, are you discussing sessions where you invited people in to provide you with information or to hear what was going on? Is that -- is that what you mean?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN KARADZIC
utterances.text: That's an expanded session. That's the case in the SDS and in the Presidency and anywhere when somebody else is in attendance too, but that is just an expanded session, not a body that's expanded and that is in session.

utterances.speaker: MR. N
utterances.text: So when these people -- you would get advice from them, they would listen, but the expanded Presidency session was not a decision-making body. Is that what I understand you to be saying?

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Your Honour, I'm sorry. And I really -- I don't like to get up but these are a series of leading questions and I would ask them to be asked in a more open fashion.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE POCAR
utterances.text: Try to be less leading but I note in the question you put you spoke at the same time of expanded Presidency and expanded session. Maybe you made some confusion in that yourself. MR. N. DERSHOWITZ:

utterances.speaker: MR. N
utterances.text: Can you explain the difference in your mind between an expanded session of the Presidency and the phrase "expanded Presidency" as it has been used?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN KARADZIC
utterances.text: An expanded session either of the Presidency or of the Main Board or of any body means that that session is attended by someone who is not a member of that body, too, for different reasons. Ministers were often in attendance, that would be an expanded session of the Presidency. However, that would not make them members of the Presidency. Also when there is a delegation of the Presidency or some body for negotiating with the Croats or the Muslims, the three of us would include a few ministers too. That would not turn them into members of the Presidency. This would mean that they are providing a service or assistance to the Presidency because the three of us cannot be the only delegation talking to the Croats or the Muslims. We have this expansion. So expanded session is attended by someone who is not a member. Expanded Presidency would have to be in the constitution which would include the Prime Minister and the president of parliament, that is to say, to have the executive and to have the legislative if the Presidency cannot function, the executive, rather.

utterances.speaker: MR. N
utterances.text: And are you then saying that the words "expanded Presidency" --

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: It's -- MR. N. DERSHOWITZ: I --

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: I understand that, and again I don't want to get up, but it's hard to imagine how a question that begins with "are you saying that" cannot be a leading question. MR. N. DERSHOWITZ: I'll phrase it differently and we'll get to the same place. I think we're just wasting some time, but I abide by the objection that was made.

utterances.speaker: MR. N
utterances.text: Can you explain the relationship, if any, between -- in your mind, between War Presidency and expanded Presidency? Are they different?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN KARADZIC
utterances.text: Well, in essence an expanded Presidency should be introduced in the war. However, we avoided this term "War Presidency." That would be the expanded Presidency if a state of war were to be declared, not in a different situation.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE POCAR
utterances.text: I'm sorry. On a technical matter, I'm advised that there is the need to change the tape and we have to break now, necessarily, for 20 minutes to allow the change of tape. MR. N. DERSHOWITZ: For 20 minutes?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE POCAR
utterances.text: Yes. MR. N. DERSHOWITZ: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE POCAR
utterances.text: The hearing is resumed. I will give the floor back to Mr. Dershowitz. MR. N. DERSHOWITZ: Thank you again, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. N
utterances.text: Mr. Karadzic, just to clarify, how many members were there of the Presidency?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN KARADZIC
utterances.text: Up until the 12th of May there were two, and from the 12th of May until the 17th of December there were three. And from then on, we transferred that into one president and two vice-presidents, and again, all three were elected by secret vote.

utterances.speaker: MR. N
utterances.text: And if there were a War Presidency or an expanded Presidency, how many members would there be of the War Presidency or expanded Presidency?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN KARADZIC
utterances.text: It would be expanded by the membership of president of the Assembly and Prime Minister and it had powers to adopt legislation because during the state of war the Assembly would not meet.

utterances.speaker: MR. N
utterances.text: And during the year 1992, were there ever any decisions, opinions, directives, orders issued by a five-person expanded or War Presidency?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN KARADZIC
utterances.text: No, not a single one. Even three of us did not vote. Rather, I asked for consent from Mrs. Plavsic and Mr. Koljevic, and if I agreed then most of our decisions were unanimous. We wouldn't adopt decisions if the decision was 2 to 1. No. I would ask for consent from each member of the Presidency.

utterances.speaker: MR. N
utterances.text: But again I'm -- what I was asking is with respect to a five-member either expanded or War Presidency. Was there ever an order, directive issued by a five-body expanded Presidency or War Presidency at any time in 1992?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN KARADZIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. N
utterances.text: You were asked a question by Mr. Tieger, and he quoted from page 100 of November, I believe he said 23rd, 1992, page 1, and I see on my screen that the quote as it's there is a little bit inaccurate, so let me try to read it slowly. I think it's the way it was taken down, not the way it was read. This is -- you were asked about this. It's a quote from Mr. Krajisnik on the 22nd of November, 1992, and it says: "Gentlemen, we have received the answer to the question by the deputy, Mr. Trbojevic, that War Presidency and the commissionary, it has been established to be unconstitutional. So if we decide that there is a need for the War Presidency and the commissionary, we should further the initiation to the constitutional committee. If we decide there is no need, then it does not have to go to the constitutional committee." And you were asked whether you knew whether Mr. Krajisnik had expressed that view, and my question to you is: Was that also your view?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN KARADZIC
utterances.text: I would like to see the original in the Serbian language. However, the essence -- I think that the essence is this: We did not have an expanded Presidency because we did not have the state of war. If that question was put forward in the parliament, then it was up to the Presidency to formulate its position, whether it needed to be expanded or whether it would continue functioning in its regular composition. If they needed it to be in the expanded form, then that question would have been sent to the constitutional commission to give its interpretation. And I think that a week later we did have a session of the Presidency and it was put forward on the agenda.

utterances.speaker: MR. N
utterances.text: Well, on the following page, page 101, the following quotation appears again from, I believe, Mr. Krajisnik. It says: "We move on to the Assembly opinion whether we need the War Presidency. The War Presidency consists of three members of the Presidency, the president of the Assembly, and the Prime Minister. Since no state of war has been declared, there is an opinion that this decision would not be constitutional. The same thing applies to the commissionary. I open the discussions." Does that confirm your recollection that there was a discussion as to whether there was a need for -- of a War Presidency or an expansion Presidency discussed in November of 1992?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN KARADZIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. N
utterances.text: And do you know whether it was ever voted upon and approved in 1992 to have a War Presidency or an expanded Presidency?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN KARADZIC
utterances.text: I don't know whether in that session a vote was taken in the parliament. I guess it wasn't because the question was sent back to us at the Presidency to declare whether we would continue functioning as the Presidency within its normal composition or whether we would ask for expansion. And then a week later, I think on 30th of November, we did have a Presidency session and concluded that there was no need for the expanded Presidency.

utterances.speaker: MR. N
utterances.text: And if there had been an expanded Presidency, under the same provisions of the constitution would there be a number of other things that would occur once there had been a declaration of a state of war?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN KARADZIC
utterances.text: Absolutely. That body would function as an integrated both legislative and executive power. It would pass legislation and issue directives and regulations aimed at the government, but at the time when the Assembly met, it would have to put on the agenda everything that had been passed in the meantime by the Presidency so that the Assembly could adopt it. And since we did have a regular parliamentary life, there was absolutely no reason for this. We had many parliamentary sessions.

utterances.speaker: MR. N
utterances.text: But would there have been a requirement for war commissioners or anything else, assuming there had been a state of war and a declaration of a war or expanded Presidency?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN KARADZIC
utterances.text: The state of war could not have been passed as a secret measure. It had to be clear to everybody, because new legislation would need to be passed, and everybody had to be aware of the consequences of their conduct. So this would be war legislation, not peacetime legislation. And this state of war would have been absolutely declared, and the parliament would not meet under those circumstances, and this body would function both as legislative and executive power.

utterances.speaker: MR. N
utterances.text: And was the legislative branch continuing to function during 1992?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN KARADZIC
utterances.text: Absolutely. We held many sessions, both in 1992 and throughout that period of conflict which we do not call a war. We call it a tragic conflict. So you can see minutes from the 1992. You can see that there were many, many parliamentary sessions.

utterances.speaker: MR. N
utterances.text: During the period from when the Presidency was expanded to three members and you became the president, through, I guess, December 30, 1992, which is the end of the indictment period, did Mr. Krajisnik continue in his efforts to negotiate?

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Sorry, Your Honour. That's within the scope of the 92 ter and not within the scope of the cross or questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE POCAR
utterances.text: I believe you should not put that question, Mr. Dershowitz. MR. N. DERSHOWITZ: Your Honour, if I may respond to the objection.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE POCAR
utterances.text: Sure. MR. N. DERSHOWITZ: The question that had been asked is whether these military objectives also included -- or whether the political objectives also constituted the military objectives. I'm trying to expand upon what the political objectives were during that period of time and whether Mr. Krajisnik was involved in the efforts on the political end, to distinguish it from the military end because that was his function. So with all due respect, I think it is clearly responsive to the questions that were asked and that's why I had it down.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Your Honour, the 92 ter raises that point. These were political objectives. Presumably with political objectives would be political negotiations. That's part of the 92 ter. In cross-examination the point was raised that they were also military objectives. That was addressed exclusively, not the political aspect. MR. N. DERSHOWITZ: Again, Your Honour, he was involved in the political. The inference was that he was also, because he was a member of the of leadership, involved in the military and I want to demonstrate that his function was the political function. So it's clearly responsive to the inquiries that had been made.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE POCAR
utterances.text: Please proceed. Bear in mind you have little time now. MR. N. DERSHOWITZ: Can you give me a rough estimate as to how much?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE POCAR
utterances.text: Ten to 15 minutes. MR. N. DERSHOWITZ: Okay. I'll take less than that. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. N
utterances.text: Can you answer the question? The question was whether he was involved in the political -- the negotiations during the period of May 1992 through December 30, 1992.

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN KARADZIC
utterances.text: The negotiations never stopped. They were continuing under the mediation of international representatives. Mr. Krajisnik, throughout the time, was a member of the negotiating team together with Minister Buha, Koljevic, and so on. So he -- there was a political process throughout that whole time. We had never lost hope that a political solution would be found, and we were prepared to return territories and to find a fair territorial solution. This has nothing to do with military goals.

utterances.speaker: MR. N
utterances.text: And to what extent was -- who else was actively involved with him in that negotiating obligations?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN KARADZIC
utterances.text: On behalf of the Presidency there were Mr. Koljevic and myself; and then on behalf of the parliament, it was Mr. Krajisnik; and then on behalf of the cabinet, it was Minister of Foreign Affairs, Mr. Buha. That means that all of us were represented, the parliament, the cabinet, and the Presidency.

utterances.speaker: MR. N
utterances.text: And were there discussions before entering into the negotiations as to what the position was of the negotiators for the Serbian side?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN KARADZIC
utterances.text: Yes, absolutely. We had to abide by the rules that the parliament set up for us, and we also had to coordinate our tactics so that we could appear as a unified delegation, and we did that before all negotiations. I couldn't change the members of the negotiating team because that would mean disrespect to the mediators, and that would also mean an obstruction of -- on our part, of the negotiations.

utterances.speaker: MR. N
utterances.text: Now, in response to the questions that you were asked about the military part, was Mr. Krajisnik in any way involved in taking the goals and objectives that you were seeking to pursue politically and turning them into a military objective?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN KARADZIC
utterances.text: There could not have been a military objective, because we knew that in the end everything had to end up with negotiations. We did not want all of the Bosnia under our control. We wanted what was offered to us by the conference. So the military goals are pointless, nor did the political leadership get involved in them, especially not the parliament.

utterances.speaker: MR. N
utterances.text: All right. But putting aside the leadership, I'm only focusing now on Mr. Krajisnik. He was involved in the political efforts at negotiating a political settlement. Was he also in any way involved in the military operations either by being in a command position, an authority position, or right to issue any orders as it applied to the military part of what was going on at that time?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN KARADZIC
utterances.text: Absolutely not. MR. N. DERSHOWITZ: May I have one moment to consult?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN KARADZIC
utterances.text: MR. N. DERSHOWITZ: Your Honour, I have no further questions, and Mr. Krajisnik tells me he does not have any further questions. Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE POCAR
utterances.text: I thank you, Mr. Dershowitz. Any questions from the Bench? Judge Shahabuddeen.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SHAHABUDDEEN
utterances.text: Only an observation, Mr. Dershowitz. I gained the impression that you -- your questions were directed to achieving this result: That you assumed that JCE was a valid concept but that you were seeking to demonstrate that on the facts there was no liability, but I thought that your -- the province of your jurisdiction was confined to attacking the concept of JCE itself. MR. N. DERSHOWITZ: Your Honour, that is a very good question. What I had in mind is the question of JCE itself. There were three questions. One is the -- the concept, the legal parameters, the descriptions of JCE. That's one province. A matter of law whether the words and phrases that have been used to describe it leave it as an open-ended concept, a concept that has problems, the lack of description, the lack of notice, lack of a predicate. All of those questions, that's "A." The second is whether or not there was a JCE at all. The third is whether or not Mr. Krajisnik, even if there was a JCE, was a member of the JCE or could be held liable for a JCE if he articulated --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SHAHABUDDEEN
utterances.text: Would you say that that third question was transacted by you in the written brief which you submitted? MR. N. DERSHOWITZ: Without a doubt. And what I was trying to do, candidly, is use the witness in order to buttress the claims that we had made that Mr. Krajisnik's function was to articulate, to be involved in negotiations, to articulate, to seek to resolve the question politically and that his views were to protect the interest of the Serbs. To the extent that he had those views and maybe others had those views and others engaged in illegality, it is inappropriate to take an individual who is expressing legitimate, justifiable, protected, encouraged statements and to make him liable for the actions of others who he doesn't control, has no power over, who engage in illegality. So I thought I can secure certain information from this witness. I believe I did secure information narrowly focused, because I didn't think this witness would be the one for JCE purposes to address the first question that I raised, nor the second question that I raised.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SHAHABUDDEEN
utterances.text: I must read over your brief more carefully to see whether it deals with these aspects. Thank you. MR. N. DERSHOWITZ: May I make a suggestion, Your Honour, with all due respect? I read over the argument the other day in anticipation of this proceeding, and I suggest that if you read over the argument that had been made and some of the questions that the Chamber had asked, I think this issue became much more focused, that it may have -- it was there, but much more focused, both in my presentation and in my brother's presentation, and I think my brother was expanding on it in terms of every other conflict that exists around the world where people take a political position and others engage in crimes in illegality. So if you're going to read it over, I request, not because I said it and not because my brother did, but I request you look at the oral argument which I think is even more focused.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SHAHABUDDEEN
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Dershowitz. MR. N. DERSHOWITZ: Thank you very much, Your Honour. Any other ...

utterances.speaker: JUDGE POCAR
utterances.text: If there are no other questions, this concludes the questioning of the witness. So I will -- the witness -- Mr. Karadzic, we thank you for your testimony, and you can be excused now and leave the courtroom accompanied by the usher --

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. President, also I would like to express my thanks to you for allowing me to appear today and for respecting the rights of my client. I think we are both very satisfied with these proceedings. Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE POCAR
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE POCAR
utterances.text: It remains now to admit into evidence the statement of Mr. Karadzic. So can I ask the registrar to proceed to that.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: The 92 ter statement of Mr. Karadzic will be Exhibit AD3, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE POCAR
utterances.text: I thank you. So this concludes this evidentiary hearing. The Chamber will now rise.

procedural_notes.text: --- Whereupon the hearing adjourned at 1.29 p.m.
